  unit-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [16.x, 18.x]
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
    - run: npm ci
    - run: npm test
    
  # Job 2: Platform matrix testing
  platform-tests:
    needs: unit-tests
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [macos-latest, ubuntu-latest]
        platform: [android, ios]
        include:
          - os: macos-latest
            platform: ios
            xcode: '15.0'
          - os: macos-latest
            platform: android
            android-sdk: '33'
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            platform: android
            android-sdk: '33'
      fail-fast: false  # Don't stop if one combination fails
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Setup ${{ matrix.platform }}
      if: matrix.platform == 'ios'
      run: |
        sudo xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode_${{ matrix.xcode }}.app
        xcodebuild -version
    
    - name: Run ${{ matrix.platform }} tests
      run: |
        if [ "${{ matrix.platform }}" = "ios" ]; then
          npm run test:ios
        else
          npm run test:android
        fi
    
  # Job 3: E2E tests on real devices (cloud)
  e2e-tests:
    needs: platform-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        device: ["iPhone 14", "Pixel 7", "Galaxy S22"]
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Run E2E tests on ${{ matrix.device }}
      uses: browserstack/github-actions@v1.0
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME }}
        access-key: ${{ secrets.BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY }}
        framework: "appium"
        device: ${{ matrix.device }}
        platform: "${{ contains(matrix.device, 'iPhone') && 'ios' || 'android' }}"
        test-suite: "./e2e-tests"
    
  # Job 4: Visual regression tests
  visual-tests:
    needs: e2e-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Run visual tests
      env:
        PERCY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PERCY_TOKEN }}
      run: |
        npm run test:visual
    
  # Job 5: Performance tests (nightly only)
  performance-tests:
    needs: visual-tests
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    runs-on: macos-latest
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Run performance benchmarks
      run: npm run test:performance
      
    - name: Upload performance results
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      with:
        name: performance-results
        path: ./performance-report.json

content.title: Test Maintenance and Flaky Test Management
content.explanation:
Cross-platform tests face unique maintenance challenges:

**Common Flakiness Sources**:
1. **Async Operations**: Network requests, animations, native bridge calls
2. **Platform Timing Differences**: iOS vs Android animation durations
3. **State Issues**: App state not resetting between tests
4. **External Dependencies**: APIs, push notifications, system dialogs

**Management Strategies**:
1. **Smart Retry Logic**:
   • Exponential backoff for network-dependent tests
   • Platform-specific retry configurations
   
2. **Test Stability Scoring**:
   • Track test failure rates over time
   • Identify and fix consistently flaky tests
   • Quarantine truly problematic tests
   
3. **Isolation Techniques**:
   • Run flaky tests in separate pipeline
   • Use mock servers to eliminate network variability
   • Clear app state between tests

content.caption: Flaky Test Management System

content.title: Real Device vs. Simulator/Emulator Strategy
content.explanation:
Choosing the right testing environment is critical for cross-platform:

**Simulator/Emulator Advantages**:
• Fast startup and execution
• Consistent behavior
• Easy to automate
• Low cost

**Real Device Necessities**:
• Hardware-specific features (camera, GPS, sensors)
• Real-world performance characteristics
• Network condition variability
• Platform-specific bugs only appear on real devices

**Testing Strategy Matrix**:
• **Unit/Component Tests**: 100% simulators/emulators
• **UI Tests**: 80% simulators, 20% real devices (critical paths)
• **Performance Tests**: 100% real devices
• **Hardware Tests**: 100% real devices (camera, GPS, biometrics)

**Cloud Device Farms**:
• BrowserStack, Sauce Labs, Firebase Test Lab
• Access to diverse real devices
• Parallel execution capabilities
• Cost-effective for occasional real device testing

content.title: Best Practices and Anti-Patterns
content.explanation:
**DO's for Cross-Platform Testing**:
✅ **Test on lowest common denominator devices**: Ensure app works on older/slower devices
✅ **Implement platform-specific test variations**: Acknowledge and test differences
✅ **Use feature flags for platform rollouts**: Control feature availability by platform
✅ **Monitor performance on both platforms**: Track platform-specific performance metrics
✅ **Test accessibility on each platform**: Platform accessibility implementations differ
✅ **Establish platform-specific baselines**: Visual, performance, and behavior baselines
✅ **Implement cross-platform reporting**: Unified dashboard showing all platforms

**DON'Ts for Cross-Platform Testing**:
❌ **Assume identical behavior across platforms**: Test differences, don't ignore them
❌ **Ignore platform-specific guidelines**: Material Design vs HIG compliance matters
❌ **Test only on simulators/emulators**: Real device testing is non-negotiable
❌ **Overlook platform-specific UI patterns**: Navigation, gestures, feedback differ
❌ **Neglect battery/performance impact**: Each platform has different optimization needs
❌ **Use platform detection as a crutch**: Design for platforms, don't just detect and patch
❌ **Forget about app store requirements**: Each store has different review criteria

items.myth: Write once, test once
items.reality: Write once, test everywhere - platform differences require verification

items.myth: Cross-platform eliminates native expertise
items.reality: You still need platform experts, just fewer of them

items.myth: One test framework covers everything
items.reality: You need a testing toolkit, not a single tool

items.myth: If it works on iOS, it works on Android
items.reality: Platform differences guarantee some issues won't crossover

items.myth: Visual tests replace functional tests
items.reality: Visual tests complement functional tests, don't replace them

tutorials.description: Understand core concepts of REST APIs, HTTP protocols, and how to validate them through automation with comprehensive testing strategies.
learningObjectives: Understand REST architectural principles and HTTP protocols
Master API testing types and methodologies

content.title: Why API Testing Matters More Than Ever
The Hidden World of APIs That Powers Everything
content.explanation:
Every time you use a mobile app, visit a website, or use any modern software, you're interacting with APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) - the invisible bridges that allow different software systems to communicate.

Think of APIs as restaurant waiters: you (the client) give your order (request), the waiter takes it to the kitchen (server), and brings back your food (response). You don't need to know how the kitchen works, and the kitchen doesn't need to know who you are. This separation allows systems to evolve independently while working together seamlessly.

As testers, APIs represent our most powerful testing surface. While UI testing tells us 'what users see,' API testing tells us 'what the system actually does.' This is where real bugs hide and where we can catch them earliest.

content.value: Real-world examples of APIs you use daily:
subpoints: Weather app: Fetches data from weather service API
Social media login: Uses OAuth API from Google/Facebook
Payment processing: Communicates with Stripe/PayPal APIs
Ride-sharing: Coordinates between user app, driver app, and mapping APIs
E-commerce: Connects product catalog, inventory, and payment APIs

content.title: How Developers Think About APIs vs How Testers Should Think
content.explanation:
Developers focus on making APIs work. Testers focus on making APIs work correctly, reliably, and securely.

Where developers ask 'Does it return data?', testers ask:
• Does it return the RIGHT data?
• Does it handle WRONG data gracefully?
• Does it perform quickly under load?
• Is it secure from attacks?
• Does it recover from failures?

This mindset shift is critical. API testing isn't about verifying functionality works - it's about ensuring the API behaves correctly in all scenarios, including the ones developers didn't anticipate.

content.title: API vs UI Testing: Strategic Comparison
rows: API for fast feedback, UI for user experience
API for core logic, UI for end-to-end flows

content.title: The Business Impact of Poor API Testing
content.explanation:
Bad APIs have real consequences:

• **E-commerce API fails** during Black Friday → Millions in lost sales
• **Banking API has security flaw** → Customer data exposed
• **Ride-sharing API is slow** → Users abandon the app
• **Payment API has race condition** → Double charges customers
• **Social media API leaks data** → Regulatory fines and brand damage

Good API testing prevents these scenarios by catching issues before they reach production. It's not a luxury - it's a business necessity.

content.title: Real API Failure Example
content.scenario: E-commerce API accepted negative quantities
content.outcome: Users could add -10 items to cart, getting paid for 'returning' non-existent items
content.prevention: API validation testing would have caught this
content.details: The UI prevented negative inputs, but direct API calls bypassed UI validation

content.title: API Types and When to Use Them
content.explanation:
Different API types serve different purposes:

**REST (Representational State Transfer)**:
• Most common for web services
• Uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
• Stateless, cacheable, layered system
• Great for CRUD operations

**GraphQL**:
• Client specifies exactly what data it needs
• Single endpoint for all operations
• Reduces over-fetching/under-fetching
• Great for mobile apps with bandwidth constraints

**gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call)**:
• Uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers
• Fast, efficient binary format
• Bi-directional streaming
• Great for microservices communication

**SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)**:
• XML-based, strict standards
• Built-in security and transaction features
• Enterprise legacy systems
• Great for financial/healthcare with strict compliance

**WebSocket**:
• Persistent, bidirectional communication
• Real-time updates
• Great for chat, notifications, live feeds

content.title: REST API Fundamentals - The Language of the Web
HTTP: The Foundation of Web Communication
content.explanation:
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is how clients and servers talk. Understanding HTTP is like understanding grammar before writing sentences.

Every HTTP interaction has:
1. **Request**: What the client sends
   • Method (GET, POST, etc.)
   • URL (where to send it)
   • Headers (metadata about the request)
   • Body (data being sent, if any)

2. **Response**: What the server sends back
   • Status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, etc.)
   • Headers (metadata about the response)
   • Body (data being returned, if any)

As testers, we need to understand each part because we'll be inspecting and validating all of them.

content.value: HTTP Methods - The Verbs of API Communication:
subpoints: GET: Retrieve data (safe, idempotent, cacheable)
POST: Create new resource (not idempotent, not cacheable)
PUT: Update/replace entire resource (idempotent)
PATCH: Partial update (not necessarily idempotent)
DELETE: Remove resource (idempotent)
HEAD: Like GET but headers only (useful for checking existence)
OPTIONS: Discover allowed methods (CORS preflight)

content.title: Status Codes: The Server's Response Language
content.explanation:
Status codes are three-digit numbers that tell the client what happened. They're grouped by first digit:

**1xx (Informational)**: Request received, continuing
• 100 Continue: Server received request headers
• 101 Switching Protocols: Client asked to switch protocols

**2xx (Success)**: Request successfully received, understood, accepted
• 200 OK: Standard success response
• 201 Created: Resource created (usually after POST)
• 204 No Content: Success but no body to return

**3xx (Redirection)**: Further action needed
• 301 Moved Permanently: Resource moved to new URL
• 304 Not Modified: Cached version still valid

**4xx (Client Error)**: Client did something wrong
• 400 Bad Request: Malformed request
• 401 Unauthorized: Authentication needed
• 403 Forbidden: No permission (even with auth)
• 404 Not Found: Resource doesn't exist
• 429 Too Many Requests: Rate limiting

**5xx (Server Error)**: Server failed
• 500 Internal Server Error: Generic server error
• 502 Bad Gateway: Upstream server error
• 503 Service Unavailable: Server overloaded/maintenance
• 504 Gateway Timeout: Upstream server timeout

content.title: Critical Status Codes for Testers
rows: Location header contains URL of created resource
Not checking the resource was actually created
Error message explains what was wrong
Returning 403 instead of 401 for missing auth
Clear explanation of why access denied
Exposing sensitive information in error messages
No sensitive data leaked in error responses
Stack traces or internal details exposed

content.title: API Components: Building a Complete Request
content.explanation:
A well-structured API request has several components:

**URL Structure**:
• Protocol (https://)
• Domain (api.example.com)
• Path (/v1/users)
• Query parameters (?page=2&limit=10)
• Fragments (#section - rarely used in APIs)

**Headers (Metadata)**:
• Content-Type: What format is the body (application/json)
• Authorization: Credentials (Bearer token123)
• Accept: What format client wants back
• User-Agent: Client identification
• Cache-Control: Caching instructions

**Request Body**:
• JSON: Most common ({"name": "John", "age": 30})
• XML: Legacy systems (<user><name>John</name></user>)
• Form-data: File uploads or web forms
• Multipart: Mixed content types

**Path vs Query Parameters**:
• Path params identify resources: /users/{id}
• Query params filter/sort: /users?active=true&sort=name

content.caption: Complete HTTP Request Example
content.code:
POST /api/v1/users HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9
Accept: application/json
User-Agent: MyTestingFramework/1.0
Cache-Control: no-cache
Content-Length: 56

{
  "name": "Jane Doe",
  "email": "jane@example.com",
  "age": 28
}

content.title: Authentication & Authorization: The Gatekeepers
content.explanation:
Authentication (who you are) and authorization (what you can do) are critical for API security:

**API Keys**:
• Simple: api_key=abc123 in query or header
• Pros: Simple to implement
• Cons: Exposed in logs, URLs; hard to rotate

**Basic Authentication**:
• username:password base64 encoded
• Header: Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz
• Pros: Standard, widely supported
• Cons: Credentials sent with every request

**Bearer Tokens (JWT)**:
• Token-based, usually JWTs (JSON Web Tokens)
• Header: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
• Pros: Stateless, can contain claims/roles
• Cons: Tokens can't be easily revoked

**OAuth 2.0**:
• Industry standard for delegated authorization
• Flows: Authorization Code, Client Credentials, etc.
• Pros: Secure, granular permissions
• Cons: Complex to implement correctly

content.title: The API Testing Pyramid: Building a Solid Foundation
content.explanation:
Like the testing pyramid for applications, API testing has layers:

**Base (Wide Foundation)**: Unit Tests
• Test individual functions/methods
• Mock external dependencies
• Fast execution (milliseconds)
• High coverage goal (80-90%)
• Example: Validation logic, data transformations

**Middle (Integration Layer)**: API Integration Tests
• Test API endpoints with real dependencies
• Use test databases, mock external services
• Medium speed (seconds)
• Coverage: Critical paths
• Example: User creation with database validation

**Top (Narrow Peak)**: End-to-End Tests
• Test complete user journeys across APIs
• Real services (or close approximations)
• Slow execution (minutes)
• Coverage: Key user flows
• Example: Complete checkout flow

The pyramid ensures we catch most bugs early (at the base) where they're cheapest to fix.

content.value: API Testing Pyramid Metrics:
subpoints: Unit Tests: 70% of tests, 10% of execution time
Integration Tests: 20% of tests, 30% of execution time
E2E Tests: 10% of tests, 60% of execution time
Goal: Catch 90% of bugs in unit and integration tests

content.title: 1. Functional Testing: Does It Work Correctly?
content.explanation:
Functional testing verifies the API implements the specified requirements:

**Positive Testing**:
• Valid inputs produce expected outputs
• Standard workflows work correctly
• Example: POST /users with valid data returns 201

**Negative Testing**:
• Invalid inputs produce appropriate errors
• Edge cases are handled gracefully
• Example: POST /users with invalid email returns 400

**Boundary Value Analysis**:
• Test at boundaries of acceptable ranges
• Example: Age field accepts 0-150, test -1, 0, 1, 149, 150, 151

**Happy Path vs Edge Cases**:
• Happy path: Typical successful scenario
• Edge cases: Unusual but possible scenarios
• Both are equally important

content.caption: Functional Test Examples

content.title: 2. Contract Testing: Does It Follow the Rules?
content.explanation:
Contract testing ensures the API implementation matches its specification:

**What is a Contract?**:
• OpenAPI/Swagger specification
• Describes endpoints, parameters, responses
• Defines data schemas (JSON Schema)
• Documents authentication, headers, etc.

**Why Contract Testing Matters**:
• Prevents breaking changes for clients
• Ensures documentation matches reality
• Catches schema violations early
• Supports API versioning

**Types of Contract Tests**:
1. **Provider Tests**: API implements the contract correctly
2. **Consumer Tests**: Client can work with the contract
3. **Compatibility Tests**: New version doesn't break existing clients

content.caption: OpenAPI Contract Example
content.code:
openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: User API
  version: 1.0.0
  description: API for managing users

paths:
  /users:
    get:
      summary: Get all users
      parameters:
        - name: limit
          in: query
          schema:
            type: integer
            minimum: 1
            maximum: 100
          description: Number of users to return
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of users
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'
    post:
      summary: Create a new user
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/UserInput'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: User created
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'

components:
  schemas:
    User:
      type: object
      required:
        - id
        - name
        - email
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
          example: 1
        name:
          type: string
          example: John Doe
        email:
          type: string
          format: email
          example: john@example.com
    UserInput:
      type: object
      required:
        - name
        - email
      properties:
        name:
          type: string
        email:
          type: string
          format: email

content.title: 3. Performance Testing: Does It Work Well Under Load?
content.explanation:
Performance testing ensures APIs meet speed and scalability requirements:

**Types of Performance Tests**:
• **Load Testing**: Normal expected load
• **Stress Testing**: Beyond normal capacity
• **Spike Testing**: Sudden traffic increases
• **Endurance Testing**: Sustained load over time
• **Scalability Testing**: Adding resources improves performance

**Key Metrics**:
• **Response Time**: How long requests take
• **Throughput**: Requests per second
• **Error Rate**: Percentage of failed requests
• **Resource Utilization**: CPU, memory, database connections
• **Concurrent Users**: How many simultaneous users supported

content.title: 4. Security Testing: Is It Safe from Attack?
content.explanation:
APIs are prime targets for attackers. Security testing includes:

**OWASP API Security Top 10**:
1. Broken Object Level Authorization
2. Broken Authentication
3. Excessive Data Exposure
4. Lack of Resources & Rate Limiting
5. Broken Function Level Authorization
6. Mass Assignment
7. Security Misconfiguration
8. Injection
9. Improper Assets Management
10. Insufficient Logging & Monitoring

**Key Security Tests**:
• **Authentication Bypass**: Try to access without proper auth
• **Authorization Testing**: Access other users' data
• **Input Validation**: SQL injection, XSS, command injection
• **Sensitive Data Exposure**: Check for PII in responses
• **Rate Limiting**: Attempt to overwhelm the API

content.caption: Security Testing Examples
content.code:
# Testing for IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
def test_idor_vulnerability():
    # Create two users
    user1_token = create_user_and_get_token('user1')
    user2_token = create_user_and_get_token('user2')
    
    # User1 creates a private document
    doc_response = requests.post(
        f'{BASE_URL}/documents',
        json={'title': 'User1 Private Doc', 'private': True},
        headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {user1_token}'}
    )
    doc_id = doc_response.json()['id']
    
    # Try to access with User2's token (should fail)
    access_response = requests.get(
        f'{BASE_URL}/documents/{doc_id}',
        headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {user2_token}'}
    )
    
    # Should return 403 Forbidden, not 200 OK
    assert access_response.status_code == 403, \
        f'IDOR vulnerability! User2 accessed User1\'s document. Got {access_response.status_code}'

# Testing for SQL injection
def test_sql_injection():
    # Try SQL injection in query parameter
    malicious_payload = "1' OR '1'='1"
    
    response = requests.get(
        f'{BASE_URL}/users',
        params={'id': malicious_payload}
    )
    
    # Should return 400 or empty result, not all users
    if response.status_code == 200:
        data = response.json()
        # If we get all users, it's vulnerable
        assert len(data) <= 1, \
            'SQL injection vulnerability! Got multiple users from injection'

# Testing rate limiting
def test_rate_limiting():
    token = get_test_token()
    headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {token}'}
    
    # Make rapid requests
    status_codes = []
    for i in range(100):  # Should trigger rate limit
        response = requests.get(f'{BASE_URL}/users', headers=headers)
        status_codes.append(response.status_code)
    
    # Should see some 429 (Too Many Requests)
    assert 429 in status_codes, \
        'Rate limiting not working - no 429 responses received'

content.title: 5. Integration Testing: Does It Work with Others?
content.explanation:
APIs rarely work alone. Integration testing verifies:

**Internal Integrations**:
• API ↔ Database: Data persistence, transactions
• API ↔ Cache: Caching behavior, cache invalidation
• API ↔ Message Queue: Async processing
• API ↔ Other Internal Services: Microservices communication

**External Integrations**:
• Third-party APIs: Payment gateways, email services
• External Databases: Data warehouses, analytics
• Webhooks: Outgoing notifications

**Testing Strategies**:
• **Real Integrations**: Use test environments of external services
• **Mocked Integrations**: Simulate external services
• **Contract Testing**: Verify interfaces between services

content.title: Tool Selection: Choosing the Right Framework
content.explanation:
Different testing frameworks suit different needs:

**JavaScript/TypeScript Ecosystem**:
• **Supertest + Jest**: Great for Express/Node.js APIs
• **Playwright/TestCafe**: Can test APIs and UI together
• **Mocha/Chai**: Traditional combination, highly flexible
• **Cypress**: Primarily UI but can do API testing

**Python Ecosystem**:
• **Requests + Pytest**: Simple, powerful, large ecosystem
• **Robot Framework**: Keyword-driven, great for non-programmers
• **Behave**: BDD style with Gherkin
• **FastAPI TestClient**: Built-in for FastAPI applications

**Java Ecosystem**:
• **RestAssured**: DSL designed for REST API testing
• **JUnit/TestNG**: Standard testing frameworks
• **Spring Boot Test**: Built-in for Spring applications
• **WireMock**: Standalone mock server

**Choosing Criteria**:
1. Team's language expertise
2. Framework learning curve
3. Integration with existing tools
4. Community support and documentation
5. Performance and scalability

content.title: Framework Comparison for Different Use Cases
Test Data Management Strategy
content.explanation:
Managing test data is one of the hardest parts of API testing:

**Approaches**:
1. **Fresh Data per Test**:
   • Create unique data for each test
   • Clean up after test
   • Pros: Tests are independent
   • Cons: Slow, complex cleanup

2. **Shared Test Data**:
   • Pre-populated test database
   • Tests use existing data
   • Pros: Fast, simple
   • Cons: Tests can interfere

3. **Hybrid Approach**:
   • Core data shared (users, products)
   • Test-specific data created fresh
   • Best of both worlds

**Data Generation Tools**:
• **Faker libraries**: Generate realistic test data
• **Factory Bot/Model Momma**: Create data with relationships
• **CSV/JSON files**: Pre-defined test data sets
• **Database seeding scripts**: Initialize test database

content.caption: Advanced Test Data Management

content.title: Request & Response Validation Patterns
content.explanation:
Validating API responses requires systematic approaches:

**Schema Validation**:
• Verify response matches expected structure
• Check data types, required fields, formats
• Use JSON Schema for comprehensive validation

**Content Validation**:
• Verify actual data values are correct
• Check calculations, transformations
• Validate relationships between fields

**Header Validation**:
• Check content-type, caching headers
• Verify security headers (CORS, CSP)
• Validate custom headers

**Performance Validation**:
• Response time within SLA
• Size of response payload
• Compression effectiveness

content.caption: Comprehensive Response Validation

content.title: Error Handling & Negative Testing Strategy
content.explanation:
APIs must handle errors gracefully. Negative testing ensures they do:

**Common Error Scenarios**:
1. **Invalid Inputs**:
   • Wrong data types (string instead of number)
   • Malformed JSON/XML
   • Missing required fields
   • Invalid formats (email, URL, date)

2. **Boundary Violations**:
   • Values outside acceptable ranges
   • String length limits
   • Array size limits
   • Decimal precision issues

3. **Authentication/Authorization Errors**:
   • Missing credentials
   • Invalid/expired tokens
   • Insufficient permissions
   • Rate limiting

4. **Resource Issues**:
   • Non-existent resources (404)
   • Already exists conflicts (409)
   • Database constraints violated
   • External service failures

5. **Server Errors**:
   • Timeouts
   • Memory issues
   • Database connection failures
   • Third-party API failures

content.code:
import pytest
import requests
import json

BASE_URL = "https://api.example.com"

class TestNegativeScenarios:
    """Test suite for API error handling"""
    
    def test_malformed_json(self):
        """Test API handles malformed JSON gracefully"""
        headers = {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
        
        # Various malformed JSON payloads
        malformed_payloads = [
            '{"name": "John", "email":}',          # Missing value
            '{"name": "John" "email": "test"}',    # Missing comma
            '{name: "John", email: "test"}',        # No quotes on keys
            '{"name": "John", "age": "thirty"}',   # Wrong type
            '',                                      # Empty body
            'not json at all',                       # Not JSON
        ]
        
        for payload in malformed_payloads:
            response = requests.post(
                f"{BASE_URL}/users",
                data=payload,
                headers=headers
            )
            
            # Should return 400 Bad Request
            assert response.status_code == 400, \
                f"Expected 400 for malformed JSON, got {response.status_code}"
            
            # Should have error message
            if response.status_code == 400:
                error_data = response.json()
                assert 'error' in error_data
                assert 'message' in error_data['error']
    
    def test_missing_required_fields(self):
        """Test API rejects requests with missing required fields"""
        # User requires name and email
        incomplete_payloads = [
            {},                                      # Empty object
            {"name": "John"},                       # Missing email
            {"email": "john@example.com"},          # Missing name
            {"age": 30},                            # Missing required fields
        ]
        
        for payload in incomplete_payloads:
            response = requests.post(
                f"{BASE_URL}/users",
                json=payload
            )
            
            assert response.status_code == 400
            
            # Error should indicate which field is missing
            error_data = response.json()
            assert 'validation' in error_data or 'errors' in error_data
    
    def test_authentication_errors(self):
        """Test various authentication failure scenarios"""
        test_cases = [
            {
                'headers': {},
                'expected_status': 401,
                'description': 'No authentication'
            },
            {
                'headers': {'Authorization': 'Bearer invalid_token'},
                'expected_status': 401,
                'description': 'Invalid token'
            },
            {
                'headers': {'Authorization': 'Bearer expired_token'},
                'expected_status': 401,
                'description': 'Expired token'
            },
            {
                'headers': {'Authorization': 'Basic invalid_base64'},
                'expected_status': 401,
                'description': 'Invalid Basic auth'
            },
        ]
        
        for test_case in test_cases:
            response = requests.get(
                f"{BASE_URL}/protected",
                headers=test_case['headers']
            )
            
            assert response.status_code == test_case['expected_status'], \
                f"{test_case['description']}: Expected {test_case['expected_status']}, got {response.status_code}"
    
    def test_rate_limiting(self):
        """Test API rate limiting"""
        token = self.get_test_token()
        headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {token}'}
        
        # Make rapid requests
        responses = []
        for i in range(150):  # Assuming limit is 100/minute
            response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/users", headers=headers)
            responses.append(response.status_code)
            
            # Small delay to avoid overwhelming
            if i % 10 == 0:
                time.sleep(0.1)
        
        # Should see some 429 responses
        assert 429 in responses, "Rate limiting not triggered"
        
        # Count rate limited responses
        rate_limited = responses.count(429)
        print(f"Rate limited {rate_limited} times out of {len(responses)} requests")
        
        # Check rate limit headers
        last_response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/users", headers=headers)
        if 'X-RateLimit-Limit' in last_response.headers:
            print(f"Rate limit: {last_response.headers['X-RateLimit-Limit']}")
            print(f"Remaining: {last_response.headers['X-RateLimit-Remaining']}")
    
    def test_concurrent_requests(self):
        """Test handling of concurrent requests"""
        import threading
        import queue
        
        results = queue.Queue()
        
        def make_request(request_id):
            """Worker thread function"""
            try:
                response = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/users/{request_id}")
                results.put({
                    'id': request_id,
                    'status': response.status_code,
                    'time': response.elapsed.total_seconds()
                })
            except Exception as e:
                results.put({'id': request_id, 'error': str(e)})
        
        # Create multiple threads
        threads = []
        for i in range(50):
            thread = threading.Thread(target=make_request, args=(i,))
            threads.append(thread)
            thread.start()
        
        # Wait for all threads
        for thread in threads:
            thread.join()
        
        # Collect results
        all_results = []
        while not results.empty():
            all_results.append(results.get())
        
        # Analyze results
        successful = [r for r in all_results if 'status' in r and r['status'] == 200]
        errors = [r for r in all_results if 'status' in r and r['status'] >= 400]
        exceptions = [r for r in all_results if 'error' in r]
        
        print(f"Successful: {len(successful)}")
        print(f"Errors: {len(errors)}")
        print(f"Exceptions: {len(exceptions)}")
        
        # Should handle concurrent requests without crashing
        assert len(exceptions) == 0, f"Exceptions during concurrent requests: {exceptions}"

content.explanation:
Contract testing ensures APIs adhere to their specifications:

**Why Contract Testing Matters**:
1. **Prevents Breaking Changes**: Catch incompatible changes before deployment

4. **Supports Versioning**: Clear contracts enable version management

openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: User API
  version: 1.0.0
  description: API for managing users

# Test-specific extensions
x-test-config:
  baseUrl: https://api.example.com
  authentication:
    type: bearer
    token: ${TEST_TOKEN}
  testData:
    users:
      valid:
        - id: 1
          name: John Doe
          email: john@example.com
        - id: 2
          name: Jane Smith
          email: jane@example.com
      invalid:
        - name: ""  # Empty name
          email: "invalid-email"

paths:
  /users:
    get:
      summary: Get all users
      operationId: getUsers
      parameters:
        - name: limit
          in: query
          schema:
            type: integer
            minimum: 1
            maximum: 100
            default: 20
          description: Number of users to return
          x-test-examples:
            valid: [1, 20, 100]
            invalid: [0, 101, "not-a-number"]
        - name: offset
          in: query
          schema:
            type: integer
            minimum: 0
            default: 0
          description: Pagination offset
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of users
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'
          x-test-examples:
            - headers:
                content-type: application/json
              body: |
                [
                  {
                    "id": 1,
                    "name": "John Doe",
                    "email": "john@example.com"
                  }
                ]
        '400':
          description: Bad request
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
          x-test-examples:
            - headers:
                content-type: application/json
              body: |
                {
                  "error": {
                    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
                    "message": "Limit must be between 1 and 100"
                  }
                }

  /users/{userId}:
    get:
      summary: Get user by ID
      operationId: getUserById
      parameters:
        - name: userId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: integer
            minimum: 1
          description: User ID
          x-test-examples:
            valid: [1, 2, 999]
            invalid: [0, -1, "abc"]
      responses:
        '200':
          description: User details
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'
        '404':
          description: User not found
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'

components:
  schemas:
    User:
      type: object
      required:
        - id
        - name
        - email
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
          example: 1
          x-test-examples: [1, 100, 999999]
        name:
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 100
          example: John Doe
          x-test-examples: ["John", "Jane Smith", "A"]
        email:
          type: string
          format: email
          example: john@example.com
          x-test-examples:
            valid: ["test@example.com", "user.name@domain.co.uk"]
            invalid: ["not-an-email", "@domain.com", "user@"]
        age:
          type: integer
          minimum: 0
          maximum: 150
          example: 30
          x-test-examples:
            valid: [0, 18, 30, 150]
            invalid: [-1, 151, "thirty"]
        createdAt:
          type: string
          format: date-time
          readOnly: true
          example: "2024-01-25T10:30:00Z"
    Error:
      type: object
      required:
        - error
      properties:
        error:
          type: object
          required:
            - code
            - message
          properties:
            code:
              type: string
              example: "NOT_FOUND"
            message:
              type: string
              example: "User not found"
            details:
              type: object
              additionalProperties: true

content.title: Mocking & Stubbing Strategies
content.explanation:
Mocking external dependencies is essential for reliable API testing:

**When to Mock**:
1. **Third-party APIs**: Payments, SMS, email services
2. **Unavailable Services**: Services under development
3. **Costly Operations**: Operations with fees or limits
4. **Flaky Services**: Services with reliability issues
5. **Edge Cases**: Testing failure scenarios

**Mocking Approaches**:
1. **Client-Side Mocking**: Intercept requests at client level
2. **Server-Side Mocking**: Replace actual service with mock
3. **Network-Level Mocking**: Intercept at network level
4. **Contract-Based Mocking**: Generate mocks from API specs

**Mocking Tools**:
• **Mock Service Worker (MSW)**: Service Worker based, works in Node and browser
• **Nock**: HTTP mocking for Node.js
• **WireMock**: Standalone mock server
• **JSON Server**: Quick mock REST API from JSON file
• **Mountebank**: Multi-protocol test doubles

content.title: CI/CD Integration for API Testing
content.explanation:
API tests must run automatically in CI/CD pipelines:

**Pipeline Stages for API Testing**:
1. **Pre-commit/Pre-push**: Fast unit and contract tests
2. **Pull Request**: Integration tests against review environment
3. **Merge to Main**: Full test suite against staging
4. **Pre-production**: Performance and security tests
5. **Post-deployment**: Smoke tests against production

**Best Practices**:
• **Fast Feedback**: Fail fast on critical issues
• **Environment Management**: Test against appropriate environments
• **Data Management**: Clean test data, use test databases
• **Parallel Execution**: Run tests in parallel when possible
• **Artifact Storage**: Save test reports, logs, performance results
• **Notification**: Alert on failures via Slack, email, etc.

content.caption: GitHub Actions API Testing Pipeline
content.code:
name: API Testing Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'  # Daily at 2 AM

env:
  NODE_VERSION: '18'
  PYTHON_VERSION: '3.10'
  API_BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.API_BASE_URL }}
  TEST_DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.TEST_DATABASE_URL }}

jobs:
  # Job 1: Code quality and unit tests (fastest)
  code-quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Setup Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}
        cache: 'npm'
    
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci
    
    - name: Run linting
      run: npm run lint
    
    - name: Run unit tests
      run: npm run test:unit
      env:
        NODE_ENV: test
    
    - name: Upload unit test results
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      if: always()
      with:
        name: unit-test-results
        path: test-results/unit/
  
  # Job 2: Contract testing (against OpenAPI spec)
  contract-tests:
    needs: code-quality
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Setup Python
      uses: actions/setup-python@v4
      with:
        python-version: ${{ env.PYTHON_VERSION }}
        cache: 'pip'
    
    - name: Install schemathesis
      run: pip install schemathesis
    
    - name: Run contract tests
      run: |
        schemathesis run \
          --base-url=${{ env.API_BASE_URL }} \
          --checks all \
          --hypothesis-max-examples=50 \
          openapi.yaml
      env:
        API_BASE_URL: ${{ env.API_BASE_URL }}
    
    - name: Upload contract test results
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      if: always()
      with:
        name: contract-test-results
        path: schemathesis-report.json
  
  # Job 3: Integration tests (against test environment)
  integration-tests:
    needs: contract-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    
    services:
      # Start test database
      postgres:
        image: postgres:14
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
          POSTGRES_DB: testdb
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Setup Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}
    
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci
    
    - name: Wait for database
      run: |
        for i in {1..30}; do
          if pg_isready -h localhost -p 5432; then
            echo "Database is ready"
            break
          fi
          echo "Waiting for database..."
          sleep 2
        done
    
    - name: Run database migrations
      run: npm run db:migrate
      env:
        DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:test@localhost:5432/testdb
    
    - name: Run integration tests
      run: npm run test:integration
      env:
        NODE_ENV: test
        DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:test@localhost:5432/testdb
        API_BASE_URL: http://localhost:3000
    
    - name: Upload integration test results
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      if: always()
      with:
        name: integration-test-results
        path: test-results/integration/
  
  # Job 4: Performance tests (run less frequently)
  performance-tests:
    needs: integration-tests
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'  # Skip for PRs
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Setup k6
      uses: grafana/setup-k6@v1
      with:
        version: latest
    
    - name: Run smoke test
      run: k6 run --vus 1 --duration 30s tests/performance/smoke.js
      env:
        API_BASE_URL: ${{ env.API_BASE_URL }}
    
    - name: Run load test
      run: k6 run tests/performance/load.js
      env:
        API_BASE_URL: ${{ env.API_BASE_URL }}
    
    - name: Upload performance results
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      if: always()
      with:
        name: performance-results
        path: |
          tests/performance/*.json
          tests/performance/*.html
  
  # Job 5: Security tests (scheduled or on demand)
  security-tests:
    needs: integration-tests
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60
    
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3
    
    - name: Setup ZAP
      run: |
        docker pull owasp/zap2docker-stable
        docker run -v $(pwd):/zap/wrk/:rw \
          -t owasp/zap2docker-stable zap-baseline.py \
          -t ${{ env.API_BASE_URL }} \
          -r security-report.html
    
    - name: Upload security report
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
      if: always()
      with:
        name: security-results
        path: security-report.html
  
  # Job 6: Generate and publish test report
  report:
    needs: [integration-tests, performance-tests]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
    - name: Download all test results
      uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
      
    - name: Generate combined report
      run: |
        npm run generate-test-report
        
    - name: Publish test report
      uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3
      if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
      with:
        github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        publish_dir: ./test-reports
        keep_files: false

content.title: Best Practices and Common Pitfalls
content.explanation:
**DO's for API Testing**:
✅ **Test the contract, not just functionality**: Verify API follows its specification
✅ **Test error scenarios**: APIs fail more often than they succeed in production
✅ **Test performance under load**: APIs must handle concurrent users
✅ **Test security thoroughly**: APIs are prime targets for attacks
✅ **Use realistic test data**: Tests should mirror production usage
✅ **Clean up test data**: Prevent test pollution between runs
✅ **Version your API tests**: Tests should evolve with the API
✅ **Monitor API tests in production**: Verify APIs work in real-world conditions

**DON'Ts for API Testing**:
❌ **Assume happy path is enough**: Edge cases cause most production issues
❌ **Test only with perfect data**: Real users provide messy, invalid data
❌ **Ignore response times**: Performance is a feature
❌ **Forget about authentication**: Security testing is non-negotiable
❌ **Hardcode test data**: Tests should be data-driven
❌ **Run all tests sequentially**: Parallel execution saves time
❌ **Ignore test maintenance**: Outdated tests give false confidence
❌ **Test only in perfect conditions**: Network issues, timeouts happen

Why Postman Has Become the API Testing Standard

Postman started as a simple Chrome extension for testing APIs and evolved into the world's most popular API platform. But here's the secret most teams miss: Postman isn't just a GUI tool - it's a complete API development lifecycle platform.

The power of Postman automation comes from its unique combination:

2. **Collections as Code**: Exportable, version-controlled test suites
3. **Newman for Automation**: Run those collections anywhere
4. **Monitoring & Documentation**: Built-in, no extra tools needed

This means developers can explore APIs visually, testers can automate those explorations, and both can collaborate on the same artifacts. No more 'testers write code, developers use curl' disconnect.

content.title: How Developers Think vs How Testers Should Think in Postman
content.explanation:
Developers often use Postman as a 'quick debug tool' - make a request, see the response, move on. Testers need to think differently:

• **Developers**: 'Does this endpoint work?'
• **Testers**: 'Does this endpoint work correctly, reliably, securely, and consistently?'

Where developers might test one happy path, testers must design comprehensive test suites covering:
• All HTTP methods on each endpoint
• Various authentication scenarios
• Edge cases and error conditions
• Performance expectations
• Security vulnerabilities

Postman makes this accessible - you don't need to be a coding expert to create sophisticated API tests.

content.title: Postman/Newman vs Code-based Automation: Strategic Choice

Many teams start with 'let's just use Postman for testing' without a strategy. This leads to:

1. **Collection Sprawl**: Dozens of unorganized collections
2. **Environment Chaos**: Variables scattered everywhere
3. **Script Duplication**: Same logic copied across tests
4. **Manual Execution**: Tests never automated
5. **No Reporting**: Results trapped in GUI

Proper Postman automation requires discipline:
• Structured collection organization
• Systematic environment management

The payoff: Tests that developers trust, that run in CI/CD, and that actually prevent bugs.

content.title: Postman Collection Architecture: Building Test Suites That Scale
Collection Structure: The Foundation of Maintainable Tests
content.explanation:
Well-structured collections are like well-organized code. A good collection structure:

1. **Logical Hierarchy**:
   • Collection (Project)
   • Folder (Module/Feature)
   • Request (Endpoint)
   • Tests (Assertions)

2. **Naming Conventions**:
   • Collection: `Product API - v1.0.0`
   • Folder: `Users Management`
   • Request: `[POST] Create User`
   • Test: `✅ Status 201 Created`

3. **Documentation**:
   • Description for each collection, folder, request
   • Example requests and responses
   • Setup instructions

Think of collections as test suites, folders as test cases, and requests as test steps.

Folder: Orders (Create, view, update, cancel)

Folder: Admin (All admin-only endpoints)
Folder: Performance (Load tests, response time checks)

content.title: Variables: The Key to Flexible, Reusable Tests
content.explanation:
Postman variables have different scopes, each with specific use cases:

**Global Variables**:
• Available across all collections
• Use for: API keys, default timeouts, company-wide settings
• Example: `company_name`, `default_timeout`

**Collection Variables**:
• Available only within a collection
• Use for: API version, base URLs for this API
• Example: `api_version`, `base_url`

**Environment Variables**:
• Switch between configurations
• Use for: Different environments (dev, staging, prod)
• Example: `api_base_url`, `database_url`

**Local Variables**:
• Temporary, request-scoped
• Use for: Loop counters, temporary calculations
• Automatically cleared after request

**Data Variables**:
• From external data files (CSV, JSON)
• Use for: Data-driven testing
• Example: Test user credentials in CSV

content.title: Pre-request Scripts: Beyond Simple Setup
content.explanation:
Pre-request scripts are where Postman automation gets powerful. They run BEFORE the request is sent and can:

1. **Generate Dynamic Data**:
   • Unique identifiers for each test run
   • Timestamps for time-sensitive operations
   • Random test data

2. **Calculate Values**:
   • Hashes for signatures
   • Encrypted tokens
   • Complex query parameters

3. **Set Up State**:
   • Get authentication tokens from previous responses
   • Prepare request bodies based on environment
   • Set headers dynamically

4. **Implement Logic**:
   • Skip tests based on conditions
   • Set up test data in database
   • Clean up from previous tests

Think of pre-request scripts as 'setup' methods in traditional testing frameworks.

content.caption: Advanced Pre-request Script Examples

content.title: Test Scripts: Comprehensive API Validation
content.explanation:
Test scripts run AFTER the request completes. This is where you validate the response. Good test scripts:

1. **Validate Structure**: Check response format, headers
2. **Validate Data**: Check values, calculations, business rules
3. **Validate Performance**: Response time, size
4. **Set State**: Extract values for subsequent requests
5. **Handle Errors**: Graceful failure with useful messages

Postman uses the Chai assertion library (same as Mocha), so you can use familiar syntax: `pm.expect(value).to.equal(expected)`

content.caption: Comprehensive Test Script Suite

content.title: Collection-Level Scripts: Orchestrating Test Flows
content.explanation:
Collection-level scripts run before the first request (Pre-request) and after the last request (Tests). These are perfect for:

**Collection Pre-request Script**:
• Initialize test run ID
• Set up global test data
• Authenticate and get tokens
• Clean up from previous runs
• Set up database state

**Collection Tests Script**:
• Aggregate results across all requests
• Calculate overall metrics
• Clean up test data
• Generate summary reports
• Set environment variables for Newman reporting

Think of these as `beforeAll` and `afterAll` in traditional testing frameworks.

content.title: Newman Architecture: How It Really Works
content.explanation:
Newman isn't just a 'Postman runner' - it's a sophisticated test execution engine:

**How Newman Executes**:
1. **Parses Collection JSON**: Understands structure, variables, scripts
2. **Sets Up Runtime**: Creates JavaScript sandbox for scripts
3. **Processes Variables**: Resolves all variable references
4. **Executes Requests**: Sends HTTP requests, handles retries
5. **Runs Scripts**: Executes pre-request and test scripts
6. **Collects Results**: Aggregates pass/fail statistics
7. **Generates Reports**: Outputs in various formats

**Key Newman Concepts**:
• **Iterations**: How many times to run the collection
• **Data Files**: External data for data-driven testing
• **Reporters**: Different output formats
• **Environments**: Switch configurations
• **Folders**: Run specific test suites

Newman brings Postman collections from the GUI to the command line, making them executable anywhere.

content.title: Newman Command Line Mastery
content.explanation:
Newman has dozens of options. Understanding them unlocks its full potential:

**Execution Control**:
• `--iteration-count`: Run collection N times
• `--delay-request`: Add delay between requests
• `--timeout-request`: Request timeout in ms
• `--timeout-script`: Script execution timeout
• `--bail`: Stop on first failure
• `--ignore-redirects`: Don't follow redirects

**Input/Output**:
• `-e, --environment`: Environment file
• `-g, --globals`: Global variables file
• `-d, --iteration-data`: Data file for iterations
• `-r, --reporters`: Which reporters to use
• `--reporter-{reporter}-export`: Output file for reporter
• `--export-environment`: Save environment after run
• `--export-globals`: Save globals after run

**Configuration**:
• `--color on/off`: Control colored output
• `--disable-unicode`: ASCII-only output
• `--verbose`: Detailed logging
• `--silent`: Minimal output

content.caption: Comprehensive Newman Command Examples
content.code:
# ===== BASIC COMMANDS =====
# Run a collection
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json

# Run with environment
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json -e Development.postman_environment.json

# Run with data file (5 iterations, one per data row)
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json -d test_users.csv -n 5

# ===== ADVANCED EXECUTION =====
# Run with delays and timeouts
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  --delay-request 1000 \
  --timeout-request 30000 \
  --timeout-script 10000 \
  --bail \
  --ignore-redirects

# Run specific folder only
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  --folder "Smoke Tests" \
  --folder "Authentication Tests"

# Run with retry on failure (custom script needed)
for i in {1..3}; do
  newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json && break || sleep 2
  echo "Attempt $i failed, retrying..."
  if [ $i -eq 3 ]; then exit 1; fi
done

# ===== REPORTING =====
# Multiple reporters with custom options
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  -r cli,json,html,junit,htmlextra \
  --reporter-json-export reports/json-report.json \
  --reporter-html-export reports/html-report.html \
  --reporter-junit-export reports/junit-report.xml \
  --reporter-htmlextra-export reports/htmlextra-report.html \
  --reporter-htmlextra-title "API Test Report - $(date +%Y-%m-%d)" \
  --reporter-htmlextra-darkTheme \
  --reporter-htmlextra-skipHeaders "Authorization" \
  --reporter-htmlextra-testPaging \
  --reporter-cli-no-summary \
  --reporter-cli-no-banner

# ===== ENVIRONMENT MANAGEMENT =====
# Export environment after run (useful for getting updated tokens)
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  -e Development.postman_environment.json \
  --export-environment updated_env.json

# Use exported environment in next run
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  -e updated_env.json

# ===== DATA-DRIVEN TESTING =====
# CSV data file
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  -d test_data.csv \
  -n 10 \
  --verbose

# JSON data file with specific structure
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  -d test_data.json \
  --iteration-data "data"  # If data is nested under "data" key

# ===== INTEGRATION WITH OTHER TOOLS =====
# Pipe output to jq for processing
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  -r json \
  --reporter-json-export - \
  | jq '.run.stats'

# Use with grep to filter results
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  --verbose 2>&1 \
  | grep -E "(FAIL|PASS|\d+ms)"

# ===== PERFORMANCE TESTING =====
# Run multiple iterations for load testing
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  -n 100 \
  --delay-request 100 \
  --suppress-exit-code \
  --reporters cli \
  --reporter-cli-no-summary \
  --reporter-cli-no-banner \
  --reporter-cli-no-failure

# ===== CUSTOM CONFIGURATION =====
# Using a Newman configuration file
echo '{
  "collection": "UserAPI.postman_collection.json",
  "environment": "Development.postman_environment.json",
  "iterationCount": 3,
  "delayRequest": 1000,
  "reporters": ["cli", "json"],
  "reporter": {
    "json": {
      "export": "report.json"
    }
  }
}' > newman-config.json

newman run newman-config.json

# ===== ERROR HANDLING =====
# Continue on error but track exit code
newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json \
  --suppress-exit-code \
  || FAILED=true

if [ "$FAILED" = true ]; then
  echo "Tests failed, but continuing..."
  # Send notification but don't fail pipeline
  curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
    --data '{"text":"API tests failed, check logs"}' \
    $SLACK_WEBHOOK
fi

# ===== PARALLEL EXECUTION =====
# Run multiple collections in parallel (using GNU parallel)
parallel newman run {} ::: \
  collections/*.postman_collection.json

# Run same collection with different environments
parallel newman run UserAPI.postman_collection.json -e {} ::: \
  environments/*.postman_environment.json

content.title: Data-Driven Testing with Newman
content.explanation:
Data-driven testing is where Newman shines. Instead of hardcoding test data, you use external files:

**CSV Format**: Simple, spreadsheet-friendly
• First row = variable names
• Subsequent rows = data values
• Use `{{variable}}` in requests

**JSON Format**: Complex, hierarchical data
• Array of objects
• Each object = one iteration
• Can nest data structures

**How It Works**:
1. Newman reads the data file
2. For each row/object, runs the collection
3. Variables from data file override other variables
4. `pm.iterationData` gives access to current row
5. Results are aggregated across all iterations

**Advanced Patterns**:
• Mix data files with environment variables
• Use multiple data files for different test suites
• Generate data files dynamically before tests
• Combine data-driven with random data generation

content.title: The Java Developer's API Testing Renaissance
Why REST Assured Is Java's API Testing Superpower
content.explanation:
REST Assured isn't just another testing library - it's a DSL (Domain Specific Language) that makes API testing in Java feel natural and expressive. For Java developers who've suffered through verbose HTTP client code, REST Assured is a revelation.

Think of REST Assured as JUnit for APIs. Where JUnit gives you `@Test`, `assertEquals()`, and `@Before`, REST Assured gives you `given()`, `when()`, `then()`, and a fluent API that reads like English.

The magic is in its design: It bridges the gap between Java's type safety and the dynamic nature of JSON/XML APIs. You get the best of both worlds - IDE auto-completion, compile-time checking, AND the flexibility to work with any API response.

content.value: What makes REST Assured special for Java teams:
subpoints: Fluent DSL that reads like natural language
Built on top of proven libraries (Hamcrest, Jackson, Groovy)
First-class JSON and XML support

Integration with JUnit, TestNG, Spring Boot
Mature, battle-tested (10+ years of development)
Active community and excellent documentation

content.title: How Java Developers Think vs How Testers Should Think in REST Assured
content.explanation:
Java developers often approach REST Assured as 'another Java library.' Testers need to think differently:

• **Developers**: 'How do I make this HTTP call?'
• **Testers**: 'How do I verify this API behaves correctly?'

Where developers might write a test that makes a request and checks status 200, testers must design comprehensive validation:
• Response structure matches contract
• Business logic is correctly implemented
• Error handling works for all scenarios
• Performance meets SLAs
• Security is properly implemented

REST Assured's fluent API makes this accessible - you're writing Java, but you're thinking like a tester.

content.title: The Hidden Power of Fluent DSLs in Testing
content.explanation:
REST Assured's `given().when().then()` syntax isn't just syntactic sugar - it's a cognitive framework that forces good test structure:

**Given**: Setup (authentication, headers, parameters, body)
**When**: Action (HTTP method and endpoint)
**Then**: Verification (assertions on response)

This pattern ensures tests are readable, maintainable, and focused. When you see a REST Assured test, you immediately understand:
1. What preconditions are needed
2. What action is being tested
3. What outcomes are expected

This is crucial for team collaboration and test maintenance. Tests that read like documentation are tests that get maintained.

content.title: Getting Started with REST Assured - Foundation First
Project Setup: Beyond Basic Dependencies
content.explanation:
Proper REST Assured setup involves more than just adding a dependency. You need:

**Core Dependencies**:
• `rest-assured`: The main library
• `json-path` / `xml-path`: For JSON/XML assertions
• `rest-assured-all`: If you want everything in one dependency

**Test Framework Integration**:
• `junit-jupiter` / `testng`: Your testing framework
• `hamcrest`: For expressive assertions (comes with REST Assured)
• `assertj-core`: Alternative to Hamcrest (optional)

**JSON Processing**:
• `jackson-databind`: For POJO mapping (highly recommended)
• `gson`: Alternative JSON processor

**Logging and Reporting**:
• `rest-assured-all` includes logging
• `allure-rest-assured`: For Allure reports
• Custom filters for logging

The key is understanding that REST Assured is modular. Include only what you need.

content.title: The Static Import Pattern: Readability vs. Namespace Pollution
content.explanation:
REST Assured relies heavily on static imports. This is a deliberate design choice:

**Why Static Imports?**
1. **Readability**: `given()` instead of `RestAssured.given()`
2. **Fluent chains**: `.body("id", equalTo(123))` reads naturally
3. **Reduced verbosity**: Less typing, more expressing

**Essential Static Imports**:
```java
import static io.restassured.RestAssured.*;
import static io.restassured.matcher.RestAssuredMatchers.*;
import static org.hamcrest.Matchers.*;
```

**The Trade-off**:
• **Pro**: Tests read like natural language
• **Con**: IDE can't easily find method origins
• **Pro**: Less boilerplate code
• **Con**: Potential namespace collisions

**Best Practice**:
• Use static imports in test classes only
• Keep production code imports explicit
• Group related static imports
• Consider using IDE templates for common imports

content.caption: Complete Static Import Strategy

content.title: Given-When-Then: The Testing Trinity
content.explanation:
The `given().when().then()` pattern is more than syntax - it's a methodology:

**Given (Arrange)**:
• Setup test preconditions
• Authentication/authorization
• Headers, parameters, cookies
• Request body
• Mock external dependencies

**When (Act)**:
• Execute the API call
• HTTP method + endpoint
• Capture the response

**Then (Assert)**:
• Validate response
• Status code, headers, body
• Performance metrics
• Business logic
• Side effects (if testing against real DB)

**And (Optional)**:
• Additional assertions
• Cleanup steps
• State verification

This pattern ensures tests are single-purpose, readable, and maintainable. Each test should test ONE thing, and the structure makes that obvious.

content.caption: Comprehensive Given-When-Then Examples

content.title: Logging Strategies: From Debugging to Reporting
content.explanation:
REST Assured has powerful logging capabilities that serve different purposes:

**Debugging Logs**:
• See what's being sent and received
• Identify malformed requests
• Debug authentication issues

**Test Reports**:
• Include request/response in test reports
• Provide context for failures
• Help non-technical stakeholders understand tests

**Performance Monitoring**:
• Log response times
• Identify slow endpoints

**Security Auditing**:
• Log authentication attempts
• Track sensitive data (be careful!)

REST Assured provides fine-grained control over what gets logged and when. You can log:
• Everything
• Only if validation fails
• Specific parts (headers, body, params)
• To different outputs (console, file, custom logger)

content.caption: Comprehensive Logging Configuration

content.title: RequestSpecification: The Blueprint for Consistency
content.explanation:
`RequestSpecification` is REST Assured's answer to DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principles. Instead of repeating the same setup in every test, you define it once and reuse it.

**What belongs in a RequestSpecification**:
• Base URL and path
• Authentication (OAuth tokens, API keys, Basic auth)
• Common headers (Content-Type, Accept, custom headers)
• Logging configuration
• SSL/TLS settings
• Proxy configuration
• Timeouts
• Filters (logging, sanitization, monitoring)

**Benefits**:
1. **Consistency**: All requests use same configuration
2. **Maintainability**: Change in one place affects all tests
3. **Readability**: Tests focus on what's unique
4. **Testability**: Easy to mock/stub different configurations

**When NOT to use RequestSpecification**:
• One-off tests with unique requirements
• Tests that need completely different configuration
• When configuration would make specs too complex

content.caption: Comprehensive RequestSpecification Patterns

content.title: ResponseSpecification: Validating Consistency
content.explanation:
While `RequestSpecification` standardizes requests, `ResponseSpecification` standardizes assertions. This ensures:

**Consistent Validation**:
• Same status codes for similar endpoints
• Consistent error response formats
• Standard performance requirements

**Maintainable Tests**:

4. **APIs**: Dynamic data from other services
5. **Java Objects**: Type-safe, IDE support

content.title: Authentication and Authorization Patterns
content.explanation:
Modern APIs use various authentication mechanisms. REST Assured supports them all:

**Basic Auth**: Simple username/password
• `auth().basic(username, password)`
• `auth().preemptive().basic(username, password)`

**Bearer Tokens**: OAuth2, JWT
• `header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)`
• `auth().oauth2(token)`

**API Keys**:
• `header("X-API-Key", key)`
• `queryParam("api_key", key)`

**OAuth2 Flows**:
• Authorization Code
• Client Credentials
• Resource Owner Password Credentials
• Implicit

**Custom Authentication**:
• Custom headers
• Cookies
• Request signing
• HMAC

**Best Practices**:
1. Never hardcode credentials in tests
2. Use environment variables or secure vaults
3. Implement token refresh mechanisms
4. Test both valid and invalid credentials
5. Verify authorization (not just authentication)

content.title: Why GraphQL Changes API Testing
content.explanation:
GraphQL isn't just another API protocol - it fundamentally changes how clients and servers communicate. Unlike REST with its fixed endpoints and responses, GraphQL gives clients the power to request exactly what they need.

For testers, this means:
• **No more over-fetching or under-fetching**: Clients specify exact fields
• **Single endpoint**: All requests go to `/graphql` instead of multiple REST endpoints
• **Type safety**: Strongly typed schema prevents many runtime errors
• **Introspection**: The API documents itself through the schema
• **Real-time capabilities**: Subscriptions for WebSocket connections

Understanding these differences is crucial for effective GraphQL testing.

content.title: The GraphQL Request/Response Cycle
content.explanation:
Understanding how GraphQL requests flow is crucial for testing:

**Request Structure**:
```json
{
  "query": "query { ... }",
  "variables": {"id": 123},
  "operationName": "GetUser"
}
```

**Response Structure**:
```json
{
  "data": {"user": { ... }},
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "Field 'invalidField' doesn't exist",
      "locations": [{"line": 3, "column": 5}],
      "path": ["user", "invalidField"]
    }
  ],
  "extensions": {}
}
```

**Key Testing Points**:
1. **Always 200 OK**: GraphQL always returns 200, even for errors
2. **Errors in response body**: Check `errors` array for issues
3. **Partial data**: You can get both `data` and `errors` simultaneously
4. **Extensions**: Custom metadata (tracing, rate limiting, etc.)

items.myth: GraphQL eliminates the need for API testing
items.reality: GraphQL changes testing but doesn't eliminate it. You still need to test queries, mutations, subscriptions, and schema

items.myth: All GraphQL responses return 200 OK
items.reality: While GraphQL itself returns 200, transport errors (network issues, timeouts) still return appropriate HTTP status codes

items.myth: GraphQL is always faster than REST
items.reality: Poorly designed GraphQL queries can be slower due to N+1 problems and over-fetching on the server side

items.myth: You don't need to test error scenarios
items.reality: Error handling is crucial in GraphQL - you need to test invalid queries, authentication errors, and business logic errors

content.title: Best Practices for GraphQL Test Automation
content.explanation:
**1. Schema-First Testing**:
Always validate against the schema first. Use introspection to ensure your tests match the current schema.

**2. Query Isolation**:
Test each field independently when possible. This helps identify which specific field is causing issues.

**3. Variable-Based Testing**:
Never hardcode values in queries. Use variables to make tests reusable and maintainable.

**4. Error Path Testing**:
GraphQL errors include a "path" field. Test that error paths correctly identify where the error occurred.

**5. Performance Baselines**:
Establish performance baselines for common queries and monitor for regressions.

**6. Subscription Testing**:
Test WebSocket connections separately from HTTP queries. Handle connection lifecycle and cleanup.

**7. Security Testing**:
Test query depth limits, rate limiting, and field-level authorization.

**8. Data Consistency**:
Ensure that mutations produce predictable, consistent results and don't break existing queries.

content.title: Why API Performance Testing is Critical
content.explanation:
API performance testing isn't just about speed - it's about reliability, scalability, and user experience under real-world conditions. A slow API can cascade into:

• **Lost revenue**: Every 100ms delay can cost 1% in sales (Amazon study)
• **Poor user experience**: Users abandon slow applications
• **Cascading failures**: One slow API can bring down entire microservices architectures
• **Hidden bottlenecks**: Issues only appear under specific load patterns

Unlike functional testing that answers "Does it work?", performance testing answers:
1. How fast does it work?
2. How many users can it support?
3. How does it behave under stress?
4. When will it break?
5. How does it recover after failure?

content.title: Performance Testing Types Comparison
rows: Before every release, to establish baselines
Max users, failure points, recovery time
Find memory leaks and resource issues
Memory usage, CPU, response time trends
Systems expected to run for days/weeks

content.title: Key Performance Metrics Decoded
content.explanation:
Understanding metrics is crucial for meaningful performance testing:

**Response Time Metrics**:
• **Average Response Time**: Useful but can hide outliers
• **Percentiles (p50, p90, p95, p99)**: More meaningful - p95 = 95% of requests faster than this
• **Max/Min Response Time**: Identify extremes

**Throughput Metrics**:
• **Requests per Second (RPS)**: How many requests the system handles
• **Transactions per Second (TPS)**: Business transactions (may involve multiple requests)
• **Data Transfer Rate**: Bandwidth usage

**Error Metrics**:
• **Error Rate**: Percentage of failed requests
• **Error Types**: Which errors occur under load

**Resource Metrics**:
• **CPU Utilization**: Should stay below 70-80% for headroom
• **Memory Usage**: Watch for leaks under endurance tests
• **Database Connections**: Connection pool saturation
• **Network I/O**: Bandwidth constraints

**User Experience Metrics**:
• **Apdex Score**: User satisfaction index (0-1)
• **Time to First Byte (TTFB)**: Perceived performance
• **Page/API Load Time**: End-to-end timing

content.title: JMeter Architecture: Beyond Basic Scripting
content.explanation:
JMeter is more than a load testing tool - it's a complete testing framework with modular architecture:

**Core Components**:
• **Test Plan**: Container for your entire test
• **Thread Groups**: Virtual user pools with scheduling
• **Samplers**: Actual requests (HTTP, JDBC, JMS, etc.)
• **Logic Controllers**: Flow control (loops, conditions, transactions)
• **Listeners**: Results collection and visualization
• **Timers**: Think times and pacing
• **Assertions**: Response validation
• **Configuration Elements**: Default settings and data
• **Pre/Post Processors**: Request/response manipulation

**Advanced Features**:
• **Distributed Testing**: Master-slave architecture for massive load
• **Cloud Integration**: BlazeMeter, Flood.io for cloud execution
• **Custom Plugins**: Extend with Java implementations
• **Correlation**: Dynamic parameter extraction
• **CSV Data Sets**: Data-driven testing at scale

**JMeter's Strengths**:
• **Mature**: 20+ years of development
• **Extensible**: Custom Java code via JSR223
• **Protocol Support**: HTTP, HTTPS, SOAP, REST, FTP, JDBC, JMS, LDAP
• **GUI + CLI**: Easy script development, efficient execution
