content.title: The Performance Testing Lifecycle
content.explanation:
Performance testing should follow a structured lifecycle to ensure comprehensive coverage and actionable results.

**7-Phase Performance Testing Lifecycle**:
```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Phase 1: Requirements] --> B[Phase 2: Planning]
    B --> C[Phase 3: Design]
    C --> D[Phase 4: Implementation]
    D --> E[Phase 5: Execution]
    E --> F[Phase 6: Analysis]
    F --> G[Phase 7: Reporting]
    G --> H[Continuous Monitoring]
```

**Phase 1: Requirements Gathering**
• **Business Requirements**: Understand business objectives and user expectations
• **Technical Requirements**: System architecture, technology stack, dependencies
• **SLAs and SLOs**: Define Service Level Agreements and Objectives
• **Non-Functional Requirements**: Performance, scalability, reliability targets
• **User Profiles**: Different user types and their behavior patterns

**Phase 2: Test Planning**
• **Test Strategy**: Overall approach and methodologies
• **Test Scenarios**: Critical user journeys to be tested
• **Load Patterns**: Ramp-up, steady-state, spike patterns
• **Success Criteria**: Quantitative metrics for test success
• **Risk Assessment**: Identify potential risks and mitigation strategies
• **Resource Planning**: Hardware, software, personnel requirements

**Phase 3: Test Design**
• **Script Development**: Create performance test scripts
• **Test Data Design**: Realistic and scalable test data
• **Environment Design**: Test environment configuration
• **Monitoring Setup**: Performance counters and metrics to monitor
• **Validation Points**: What to validate during test execution

**Phase 4: Implementation**
• **Environment Setup**: Configure test environment
• **Data Preparation**: Generate and load test data
• **Script Validation**: Verify scripts work correctly
• **Monitoring Configuration**: Set up monitoring tools
• **Dry Runs**: Execute small-scale tests to validate setup

**Phase 5: Test Execution**
• **Baseline Tests**: Establish performance baseline
• **Load Tests**: Execute planned load scenarios
• **Stress Tests**: Push system beyond limits
• **Endurance Tests**: Long-running tests for stability
• **Spike Tests**: Sudden load increase tests
• **Results Collection**: Gather all performance data

**Phase 6: Results Analysis**
• **Data Analysis**: Analyze collected performance data
• **Bottleneck Identification**: Identify performance bottlenecks
• **Root Cause Analysis**: Determine causes of performance issues
• **Trend Analysis**: Identify performance trends and patterns
• **Recommendations**: Suggest improvements and optimizations

**Phase 7: Reporting and Monitoring**
• **Test Reports**: Comprehensive performance test reports
• **Stakeholder Communication**: Share results with stakeholders
• **Action Items**: Define follow-up actions and owners
• **Knowledge Base**: Document lessons learned and best practices
• **Continuous Monitoring**: Implement ongoing performance monitoring

content.title: Realistic Load Modeling and User Simulation
content.explanation:
Creating realistic load models is critical for meaningful performance test results. Unrealistic load patterns can lead to false conclusions and missed bottlenecks.

**Components of Realistic Load Modeling**:

**1. User Behavior Patterns**:
• **Think Time**: Time between user actions (typically 2-5 seconds)
• **Page View Distribution**: Not all pages are visited equally
• **Session Length**: Typical user session duration
• **Abandonment Rates**: Users who leave without completing actions
• **Peak/Off-Peak Patterns**: Traffic varies by time of day, day of week

**2. Traffic Distribution Models**:
• **Geographic Distribution**: Users from different locations
• **Device Distribution**: Desktop, mobile, tablet usage
• **Browser Distribution**: Different browsers and versions
• **Network Conditions**: Various connection speeds and latencies

**3. Data Variability**:
• **Unique Users**: Avoid repeated use of same credentials
• **Dynamic Data**: Use different data for each virtual user
• **Cache Considerations**: Account for cache hit/miss ratios
• **Session Data**: Realistic session data and state

**Common Load Patterns**:
```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Load Patterns"
        A[Steady State] --> B[Ramp Up/Down]
        B --> C[Spike/Burst]
        C --> D[Step Load]
        D --> E[Soak/Long Running]
    end
```

**Creating Realistic User Scenarios**:
1. **Analyze Production Traffic**: Use analytics data to understand real user behavior
2. **User Segmentation**: Identify different user types (browsers, buyers, admins)
3. **Journey Mapping**: Map critical user journeys from start to completion
4. **Failure Scenarios**: Include error scenarios and edge cases
5. **Think Time Distribution**: Use statistical distributions (normal, log-normal)

**Example: E-commerce Load Model**:
• **70%**: Browsers - view products, search, browse categories
• **20%**: Shoppers - add to cart, view cart, update quantities
• **8%**: Buyers - complete checkout, make purchases
• **2%**: Admins - manage products, view reports

**Tools for Load Modeling**:
• **JMeter**: CSV Data Set, Random Variable, Gaussian Random Timer
• **Gatling**: Feeders, scenario chains, pacing
• **k6**: Scenarios, executors, think time functions
• **Custom Scripts**: Python/R for complex statistical distributions

content.caption: Advanced Load Pattern Generator
content.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Advanced Load Pattern Generator
Creates realistic load patterns for performance testing
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple, Optional
from dataclasses import dataclass
import json

@dataclass
class LoadPatternConfig:
    """Configuration for load pattern generation"""
    pattern_type: str  # steady, ramp, spike, step, soak, daily_pattern
    duration_minutes: int
    target_users: int
    start_users: int = 0
    spike_multiplier: float = 3.0
    step_increment: int = 100
    step_duration_minutes: int = 5
    think_time_mean: float = 3.0  # seconds
    think_time_std: float = 1.0
    
class LoadPatternGenerator:
    """Generates realistic load patterns for performance testing"""
    
    def __init__(self, seed: Optional[int] = None):
        if seed is not None:
            np.random.seed(seed)
    
    def generate_steady_pattern(self, config: LoadPatternConfig) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Generate steady-state load pattern"""
        timestamps = self._generate_timestamps(config.duration_minutes)
        
        # Steady load with minor variations
        base_load = config.target_users
        variations = np.random.normal(0, base_load * 0.1, len(timestamps))
        users = np.maximum(base_load + variations, 0).astype(int)
        
        return pd.DataFrame({
            'timestamp': timestamps,
            'concurrent_users': users,
            'pattern_type': 'steady'
        })
    
    def generate_ramp_pattern(self, config: LoadPatternConfig) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Generate ramp-up/ramp-down pattern"""
        timestamps = self._generate_timestamps(config.duration_minutes)
        
        # Linear ramp from start_users to target_users and back
        half_duration = len(timestamps) // 2
        
        ramp_up = np.linspace(config.start_users, config.target_users, half_duration)
        ramp_down = np.linspace(config.target_users, config.start_users, len(timestamps) - half_duration)
        users = np.concatenate([ramp_up, ramp_down]).astype(int)
        
        # Add minor noise
        noise = np.random.normal(0, config.target_users * 0.05, len(users))
        users = np.maximum(users + noise, 0).astype(int)
        
        return pd.DataFrame({
            'timestamp': timestamps,
            'concurrent_users': users,
            'pattern_type': 'ramp'
        })
    
    def generate_spike_pattern(self, config: LoadPatternConfig) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Generate spike/burst pattern"""
        timestamps = self._generate_timestamps(config.duration_minutes)
        users = np.full(len(timestamps), config.start_users)
        
        # Create spike in the middle
        spike_start = len(timestamps) // 3
        spike_duration = len(timestamps) // 6  # Spike lasts 1/6 of total duration
        
        for i in range(spike_duration):
            pos = spike_start + i
            if pos < len(users):
                # Gaussian spike shape
                spike_factor = np.exp(-((i - spike_duration/2) ** 2) / (2 * (spike_duration/4) ** 2))
                users[pos] = config.start_users + (config.target_users * config.spike_multiplier - config.start_users) * spike_factor
        
        # Add noise
        noise = np.random.normal(0, config.target_users * 0.1, len(users))
        users = np.maximum(users + noise, 0).astype(int)
        
        return pd.DataFrame({
            'timestamp': timestamps,
            'concurrent_users': users,
            'pattern_type': 'spike'
        })
    
    def generate_step_pattern(self, config: LoadPatternConfig) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Generate step load pattern"""
        timestamps = self._generate_timestamps(config.duration_minutes)
        
        # Calculate number of steps
        steps_needed = (config.target_users - config.start_users) / config.step_increment
        step_duration_points = int((config.step_duration_minutes * 60) / 5)  # Points per step
        
        users = []
        current_users = config.start_users
        
        while len(users) < len(timestamps):
            # Stay at current level for step duration
            users.extend([current_users] * min(step_duration_points, len(timestamps) - len(users)))
            
            # Increment for next step
            if current_users < config.target_users:
                current_users = min(current_users + config.step_increment, config.target_users)
            else:
                # Once at target, stay there
                users.extend([current_users] * (len(timestamps) - len(users)))
                break
        
        # Convert to array and add noise
        users_array = np.array(users[:len(timestamps)])
        noise = np.random.normal(0, config.target_users * 0.05, len(users_array))
        users_array = np.maximum(users_array + noise, 0).astype(int)
        
        return pd.DataFrame({
            'timestamp': timestamps[:len(users_array)],
            'concurrent_users': users_array,
            'pattern_type': 'step'
        })
    
    def generate_daily_pattern(self, config: LoadPatternConfig) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Generate realistic daily traffic pattern"""
        timestamps = self._generate_timestamps(config.duration_minutes, include_date=True)
        
        users = []
        for ts in timestamps:
            hour = ts.hour
            minute = ts.minute / 60.0
            
            # Base pattern: low at night, peaks during business hours
            # Using combination of sine waves to create realistic pattern
            
            # Daily rhythm (peak during day)
            daily = np.sin((hour + minute - 9) * np.pi / 12)  # Peak at 3PM
            daily = max(daily, 0)  # No negative values
            
            # Lunch dip
            lunch_dip = 0.7 if 12 <= hour + minute < 13.5 else 1.0
            
            # Evening surge
            evening = 1.2 if 18 <= hour + minute < 22 else 1.0
            
            # Combine factors
            base_load = config.target_users * daily * lunch_dip * evening
            
            # Add random variation
            variation = np.random.normal(0, base_load * 0.15)
            users.append(max(base_load + variation, 0))
        
        users_array = np.array(users).astype(int)
        
        return pd.DataFrame({
            'timestamp': timestamps,
            'concurrent_users': users_array,
            'pattern_type': 'daily'
        })
    
    def generate_think_times(self, num_actions: int, mean: float = 3.0, std: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray:
        """Generate realistic think times between user actions"""
        # Use log-normal distribution (realistic for human wait times)
        # Convert mean and std to log-normal parameters
        mu = np.log(mean**2 / np.sqrt(std**2 + mean**2))
        sigma = np.sqrt(np.log(1 + (std**2 / mean**2)))
        
        think_times = np.random.lognormal(mu, sigma, num_actions)
        
        # Cap extreme values
        think_times = np.minimum(think_times, 30)  # Cap at 30 seconds
        think_times = np.maximum(think_times, 0.1)  # Minimum 0.1 seconds
        
        return think_times
    
    def generate_user_scenarios(self, user_types: Dict[str, float], total_users: int) -> Dict[str, int]:
        """Generate user distribution across different user types"""
        # Normalize percentages
        total_percentage = sum(user_types.values())
        normalized = {k: v/total_percentage for k, v in user_types.items()}
        
        # Allocate users
        allocations = {}
        remaining_users = total_users
        
        for i, (user_type, percentage) in enumerate(normalized.items()):
            if i == len(normalized) - 1:
                # Last type gets remaining users
                allocations[user_type] = remaining_users
            else:
                allocated = int(total_users * percentage)
                allocations[user_type] = allocated
                remaining_users -= allocated
        
        return allocations
    
    def create_load_test_plan(self, patterns: List[LoadPatternConfig], 
                            user_distribution: Dict[str, float]) -> Dict:
        """Create comprehensive load test plan"""
        test_plan = {
            'metadata': {
                'created_at': datetime.now().isoformat(),
                'total_duration_minutes': sum(p.duration_minutes for p in patterns),
                'user_distribution': user_distribution
            },
            'phases': []
        }
        
        current_time = datetime.now()
        
        for i, pattern_config in enumerate(patterns):
            # Generate pattern data
            pattern_method = getattr(self, f'generate_{pattern_config.pattern_type}_pattern')
            pattern_data = pattern_method(pattern_config)
            
            # Calculate user distribution for this phase
            avg_users = pattern_data['concurrent_users'].mean()
            user_allocation = self.generate_user_scenarios(user_distribution, int(avg_users))
            
            phase = {
                'phase_number': i + 1,
                'pattern_type': pattern_config.pattern_type,
                'duration_minutes': pattern_config.duration_minutes,
                'target_users': pattern_config.target_users,
                'start_time': current_time.isoformat(),
                'user_distribution': user_allocation,
                'think_time_mean': pattern_config.think_time_mean,
                'think_time_std': pattern_config.think_time_std,
                'sample_data': {
                    'timestamps': pattern_data['timestamp'].astype(str).tolist()[:10],
                    'users': pattern_data['concurrent_users'].tolist()[:10]
                }
            }
            
            test_plan['phases'].append(phase)
            current_time += timedelta(minutes=pattern_config.duration_minutes)
        
        return test_plan
    
    def visualize_patterns(self, patterns_data: List[pd.DataFrame], output_file: Optional[str] = None):
        """Visualize load patterns"""
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(patterns_data), 1, figsize=(12, 4*len(patterns_data)))
        
        if len(patterns_data) == 1:
            axes = [axes]
        
        for i, (pattern_data, ax) in enumerate(zip(patterns_data, axes)):
            pattern_type = pattern_data['pattern_type'].iloc[0]
            
            # Convert timestamps to minutes for x-axis
            if pattern_type == 'daily':
                x_values = pattern_data['timestamp'].dt.hour + pattern_data['timestamp'].dt.minute/60
                x_label = 'Hour of Day'
            else:
                x_values = range(len(pattern_data))
                x_label = 'Time (5-second intervals)'
            
            ax.plot(x_values, pattern_data['concurrent_users'], 'b-', linewidth=2)
            ax.fill_between(x_values, 0, pattern_data['concurrent_users'], alpha=0.3)
            
            ax.set_xlabel(x_label)
            ax.set_ylabel('Concurrent Users')
            ax.set_title(f'Load Pattern: {pattern_type.title()}')
            ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
            
            # Add statistics
            stats_text = (
                f'Mean: {pattern_data["concurrent_users"].mean():.0f} users\n'
                f'Max: {pattern_data["concurrent_users"].max():.0f} users\n'
                f'Min: {pattern_data["concurrent_users"].min():.0f} users'
            )
            ax.text(0.02, 0.98, stats_text, transform=ax.transAxes,
                   verticalalignment='top',
                   bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='wheat', alpha=0.5))
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        
        if output_file:
            plt.savefig(output_file, dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
            print(f"Visualization saved to {output_file}")
        else:
            plt.show()
    
    def export_to_jmeter(self, patterns_data: List[pd.DataFrame], output_file: str):
        """Export load patterns to JMeter CSV format"""
        combined_data = pd.concat(patterns_data, ignore_index=True)
        
        # Create JMeter-friendly format
        jmeter_data = pd.DataFrame({
            'ThreadGroup.num_threads': combined_data['concurrent_users'],
            'ThreadGroup.ramp_time': 1,  # 1 second ramp between changes
            'ThreadGroup.duration': 300,  # 5 minutes per measurement
            'timestamp': combined_data['timestamp']
        })
        
        jmeter_data.to_csv(output_file, index=False)
        print(f"JMeter load pattern exported to {output_file}")
    
    def _generate_timestamps(self, duration_minutes: int, include_date: bool = False) -> List:
        """Generate timestamps at 5-second intervals"""
        num_intervals = (duration_minutes * 60) // 5
        
        if include_date:
            base_time = datetime.now().replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
            return [base_time + timedelta(seconds=i*5) for i in range(num_intervals)]
        else:
            return list(range(num_intervals))

# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    generator = LoadPatternGenerator(seed=42)
    
    # Define test phases
    phases = [
        LoadPatternConfig(
            pattern_type='ramp',
            duration_minutes=10,
            target_users=1000,
            start_users=0
        ),
        LoadPatternConfig(
            pattern_type='steady',
            duration_minutes=30,
            target_users=1000
        ),
        LoadPatternConfig(
            pattern_type='spike',
            duration_minutes=5,
            target_users=1000,
            spike_multiplier=3.0
        ),
        LoadPatternConfig(
            pattern_type='daily',
            duration_minutes=1440,  # 24 hours
            target_users=1000
        )
    ]
    
    # Generate patterns
    patterns_data = []
    for phase in phases:
        method_name = f'generate_{phase.pattern_type}_pattern'
        method = getattr(generator, method_name)
        pattern_data = method(phase)
        patterns_data.append(pattern_data)
        
        print(f"Generated {phase.pattern_type} pattern:")
        print(f"  Duration: {phase.duration_minutes} minutes")
        print(f"  Target users: {phase.target_users}")
        print(f"  Mean concurrent users: {pattern_data['concurrent_users'].mean():.0f}")
        print()
    
    # Define user distribution (e-commerce example)
    user_distribution = {
        'browsers': 0.70,    # 70% browsing users
        'shoppers': 0.20,    # 20% shopping users
        'buyers': 0.08,      # 8% buying users
        'admins': 0.02       # 2% admin users
    }
    
    # Create comprehensive test plan
    test_plan = generator.create_load_test_plan(phases, user_distribution)
    
    # Save test plan
    with open('load_test_plan.json', 'w') as f:
        json.dump(test_plan, f, indent=2)
    print("Test plan saved to load_test_plan.json")
    
    # Generate think times example
    think_times = generator.generate_think_times(1000, mean=3.0, std=1.0)
    print(f"\nThink Times Example (1000 samples):")
    print(f"  Mean: {think_times.mean():.2f} seconds")
    print(f"  Std: {think_times.std():.2f} seconds")
    print(f"  Min: {think_times.min():.2f} seconds")
    print(f"  Max: {think_times.max():.2f} seconds")
    
    # Visualize patterns
    generator.visualize_patterns(patterns_data, 'load_patterns.png')
    
    # Export to JMeter format
    generator.export_to_jmeter(patterns_data, 'jmeter_load_pattern.csv')
    
    # Print summary
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("LOAD TEST PLAN SUMMARY")
    print("="*60)
    print(f"Total duration: {test_plan['metadata']['total_duration_minutes']} minutes")
    print(f"User distribution: {user_distribution}")
    print("\nPhases:")
    for i, phase in enumerate(test_plan['phases']):
        print(f"  {i+1}. {phase['pattern_type'].title()} - {phase['duration_minutes']} minutes - ~{phase['target_users']} users")

content.title: JMeter Internal Architecture
content.explanation:
Understanding JMeter's internal architecture is crucial for building efficient test plans and troubleshooting complex scenarios.

**JMeter Core Components**:
```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Test Execution Engine"
        A[Thread Pool] --> B[Thread Group]
        B --> C[Sampler Controller]
        C --> D[Request Processing]
        D --> E[Response Processing]
    end
    
    subgraph "Processing Pipeline"
        F[Pre-Processors] --> D
        D --> G[Post-Processors]
        E --> H[Assertions]
        G --> I[Timers & Think Times]
    end
    
    subgraph "Result Collection"
        J[Sample Result] --> K[Sample Sender]
        K --> L[Backend Listeners]
        L --> M[Result Storage]
    end
    
    subgraph "External Systems"
        N[Distributed Controllers]
        O[External Data Sources]
        P[Monitoring Systems]
    end
    
    M --> P
    N --> A
    O --> F
```

**Key Architectural Concepts**:
• **Thread Model**: JMeter uses Java threads with configurable thread pooling
• **Request Lifecycle**: Each request goes through configurable processing stages
• **Memory Management**: Understanding heap usage and garbage collection patterns
• **Result Collection**: Different backends for storing test results (JTL, databases, etc.)
• **Plugin System**: Extensible architecture for custom components

**Performance Implications**:
1. **Thread Count vs Memory**: Each thread consumes ~1MB memory plus response buffers
2. **Listener Overhead**: GUI listeners can consume 30-40% of test execution time
3. **Result Storage**: File-based vs database storage trade-offs
4. **Network Latency**: Impact on distributed testing architectures

options: Thread stack size and response buffer allocation
interactive.explanation: Each JMeter thread consumes memory primarily for its thread stack (default 1MB) and response buffers. This can be tuned via JVM parameters like -Xss for stack size.

content.title: Distributed Testing Architecture for 10000+ Users
content.explanation:
Distributed testing in JMeter involves coordinating multiple load generator machines to simulate high user loads beyond a single machine's capacity.

**Architecture Components**:
```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Control Plane"
        A[JMeter Master]
        B[Test Orchestrator]
        C[Result Aggregator]
        D[Monitoring Dashboard]
    end
    
    subgraph "Load Generation Clusters"
        subgraph "Region 1"
            E[Slave Node 1]
            F[Slave Node 2]
        end
        subgraph "Region 2"
            G[Slave Node 3]
            H[Slave Node 4]
        end
    end
    
    subgraph "Infrastructure"
        I[Container Orchestrator]
        J[Cloud Providers]
        K[Network Configuration]
    end
    
    A --> E
    A --> F
    A --> G
    A --> H
    B --> I
    I --> E
    I --> F
    I --> G
    I --> H
    E --> C
    F --> C
    G --> C
    H --> C
    C --> D
```

**Key Considerations for 10000+ Users**:
1. **Network Bandwidth**: Each user requires ~50-100Kbps, totaling 500-1000Mbps
2. **Machine Specifications**: 16+ cores, 32GB+ RAM per slave for optimal performance
3. **Coordination Overhead**: Master-slave communication adds 5-10% overhead
4. **Result Aggregation**: Centralized result collection requires high I/O capacity
5. **Geographic Distribution**: Consider network latency for multi-region testing

**Scaling Formula**:
```
Total Users = ∑(Slave_i_capacity)
Slave Capacity = min(
    Threads per slave based on CPU,
    Memory limit / Memory per thread,
    Network bandwidth / Bandwidth per user
)
```

content.code:
#!/bin/bash

# Distributed JMeter Test Orchestrator
# Supports auto-scaling, result aggregation, and monitoring

set -e

# Configuration
TEST_PLAN="ecommerce-load-test.jmx"
RESULTS_DIR="/results/$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
SLAVE_COUNT=5
TARGET_USERS=10000
DURATION_MINUTES=30

# Load environment configuration
source ./jmeter-config.env

# Function to scale slaves
scale_slaves() {
    local required_slaves=$1
    echo "Scaling to $required_slaves slaves..."
    
    # Kubernetes scaling
    kubectl scale deployment jmeter-slaves --replicas=$required_slaves
    
    # Wait for slaves to be ready
    echo "Waiting for slaves to be ready..."
    while true; do
        ready_pods=$(kubectl get pods -l app=jmeter,role=slave -o jsonpath='{.items[?(@.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status=="True")].metadata.name}' | wc -w)
        if [ $ready_pods -eq $required_slaves ]; then
            break
        fi
        sleep 5
    done
}

# Function to get slave IPs
get_slave_ips() {
    kubectl get pods -l app=jmeter,role=slave -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}' | tr ' ' ','
}

# Function to run distributed test
run_distributed_test() {
    local slave_ips=$1
    local users_per_slave=$2
    
    echo "Starting distributed test with slaves: $slave_ips"
    echo "Users per slave: $users_per_slave"
    
    # Create results directory
    mkdir -p "$RESULTS_DIR"
    
    # Run JMeter in distributed mode
    /opt/apache-jmeter-5.6/bin/jmeter -n \
        -t "$TEST_PLAN" \
        -l "$RESULTS_DIR/results.jtl" \
        -e -o "$RESULTS_DIR/report" \
        -Jusers=$users_per_slave \
        -Jduration=$((DURATION_MINUTES * 60)) \
        -R "$slave_ips" \
        -Jremote_hosts="$slave_ips" \
        -Dclient.rmi.localport=60000 \
        -Dserver.rmi.ssl.disable=true
    
    # Check exit code
    if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
        echo "Test completed successfully"
        return 0
    else
        echo "Test failed"
        return 1
    fi
}

# Function to collect and analyze results
analyze_results() {
    local results_dir=$1
    
    echo "Analyzing results from $results_dir..."
    
    # Generate summary report
    /opt/apache-jmeter-5.6/bin/JMeterPluginsCMD.sh \
        --generate-csv "$results_dir/summary.csv" \
        --input-jtl "$results_dir/results.jtl" \
        --plugin-type AggregateReport
    
    # Generate response times distribution
    /opt/apache-jmeter-5.6/bin/JMeterPluginsCMD.sh \
        --generate-csv "$results_dir/response_times.csv" \
        --input-jtl "$results_dir/results.jtl" \
        --plugin-type ResponseTimesDistribution
    
    # Generate transactions per second
    /opt/apache-jmeter-5.6/bin/JMeterPluginsCMD.sh \
        --generate-csv "$results_dir/tps.csv" \
        --input-jtl "$results_dir/results.jtl" \
        --plugin-type TransactionsPerSecond
    
    # Check SLA compliance
    check_sla "$results_dir/summary.csv"
}

# Function to check SLA compliance
check_sla() {
    local summary_file=$1
    
    # Read summary CSV and check thresholds
    while IFS=, read -r label samples avg min max error_rate throughput received sent; do
        # Skip header
        if [[ "$label" == "Label" ]]; then
            continue
        fi
        
        # Convert error rate to percentage
        error_pct=$(echo "$error_rate * 100" | bc)
        
        # Check thresholds
        if (( $(echo "$error_pct > 1.0" | bc -l) )); then
            echo "ERROR: SLA violation - Error rate $error_pct% > 1% for $label"
            return 1
        fi
        
        if (( $(echo "$avg > 2000" | bc -l) )); then
            echo "WARNING: Response time $avg ms > 2000 ms for $label"
        fi
    done < "$summary_file"
    
    echo "All SLAs met successfully"
    return 0
}

# Function to upload results to cloud storage
upload_results() {
    local results_dir=$1
    
    echo "Uploading results to cloud storage..."
    
    # Upload to S3 (example)
    aws s3 sync "$results_dir" "s3://jmeter-results-bucket/$(basename $results_dir)/"
    
    # Generate and upload report URL
    local report_url="https://jmeter-reports.example.com/$(basename $results_dir)/report/index.html"
    echo "Report available at: $report_url"
    
    # Send notification
    send_notification "Test completed" "Report: $report_url"
}

# Main execution
main() {
    echo "=== Distributed JMeter Test Orchestrator ==="
    echo "Target Users: $TARGET_USERS"
    echo "Duration: $DURATION_MINUTES minutes"
    
    # Calculate required slaves
    local users_per_slave=2000  # Adjust based on capacity
    local required_slaves=$(( (TARGET_USERS + users_per_slave - 1) / users_per_slave ))
    
    echo "Required slaves: $required_slaves"
    
    # Scale slaves
    scale_slaves $required_slaves
    
    # Get slave IPs
    local slave_ips=$(get_slave_ips)
    
    # Run test
    if run_distributed_test "$slave_ips" $users_per_slave; then
        echo "Test execution successful"
        
        # Analyze results
        analyze_results "$RESULTS_DIR"
        
        # Upload results
        upload_results "$RESULTS_DIR"
        
        echo "=== Test completed successfully ==="
        exit 0
    else
        echo "=== Test failed ==="
        exit 1
    fi
}

# Execute main function
main "$@"

content.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
AI-Powered JMeter Results Analysis with Anomaly Detection and Predictive Analytics
"""

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import json
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple

# ML Libraries
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from prophet import Prophet
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

class PerformanceAnalyzer:
    """Advanced performance analysis with AI/ML capabilities"""
    
    def __init__(self, results_path: str):
        self.results_path = Path(results_path)
        self.results = None
        self.models = {}
        self.scaler = StandardScaler()
        
    def load_jmeter_results(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Load and parse JMeter results"""
        # Parse JTL/CSV results
        if self.results_path.suffix == '.jtl':
            df = pd.read_csv(self.results_path, 
                           sep=',',
                           parse_dates=['timeStamp'],
                           infer_datetime_format=True)
        elif self.results_path.suffix == '.csv':
            df = pd.read_csv(self.results_path)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported file format: {self.results_path.suffix}")
        
        # Convert timestamp
        if 'timeStamp' in df.columns:
            df['timestamp'] = pd.to_datetime(df['timeStamp'], unit='ms')
            df['hour'] = df['timestamp'].dt.hour
            df['minute'] = df['timestamp'].dt.minute
        
        self.results = df
        return df
    
    def detect_anomalies(self, features: List[str] = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Detect performance anomalies using Isolation Forest"""
        if features is None:
            features = ['elapsed', 'Latency', 'Connect']
        
        # Prepare features
        feature_data = self.results[features].dropna()
        scaled_features = self.scaler.fit_transform(feature_data)
        
        # Train anomaly detection model
        iso_forest = IsolationForest(
            n_estimators=100,
            contamination=0.05,  # Expect 5% anomalies
            random_state=42
        )
        
        anomalies = iso_forest.fit_predict(scaled_features)
        self.results['anomaly'] = anomalies
        self.results['anomaly_score'] = iso_forest.decision_function(scaled_features)
        
        # Classify anomalies
        self.results['is_anomaly'] = self.results['anomaly'] == -1
        
        return self.results
    
    def predict_performance(self, horizon_hours: int = 24) -> Dict:
        """Predict future performance using Prophet"""
        # Aggregate data by time
        hourly_data = self.results.groupby(
            pd.Grouper(key='timestamp', freq='H')
        ).agg({
            'elapsed': 'mean',
            'success': 'mean',
            'Latency': 'mean',
            'Connect': 'mean'
        }).reset_index()
        
        # Prepare for Prophet
        prophet_data = hourly_data[['timestamp', 'elapsed']].rename(
            columns={'timestamp': 'ds', 'elapsed': 'y'}
        )
        
        # Train Prophet model
        model = Prophet(
            daily_seasonality=True,
            weekly_seasonality=True,
            yearly_seasonality=False,
            changepoint_prior_scale=0.05
        )
        model.fit(prophet_data)
        
        # Make predictions
        future = model.make_future_dataframe(
            periods=horizon_hours,
            freq='H',
            include_history=True
        )
        forecast = model.predict(future)
        
        self.models['prophet'] = model
        
        return {
            'forecast': forecast,
            'model': model,
            'components': model.predictive_samples(future)
        }
    
    def analyze_performance_patterns(self) -> Dict:
        """Analyze performance patterns and trends"""
        patterns = {}
        
        # Time-based patterns
        hourly_pattern = self.results.groupby('hour').agg({
            'elapsed': ['mean', 'std', 'count'],
            'success': 'mean',
            'anomaly_score': 'mean'
        })
        
        # Response time distribution
        elapsed_stats = self.results['elapsed'].describe()
        
        # Error patterns
        error_patterns = self.results[self.results['success'] == False].groupby('Label').agg({
            'elapsed': ['count', 'mean'],
            'responseCode': lambda x: x.mode()[0] if not x.empty else None
        })
        
        patterns.update({
            'hourly_performance': hourly_pattern.to_dict(),
            'response_time_stats': elapsed_stats.to_dict(),
            'error_analysis': error_patterns.to_dict(),
            'anomaly_summary': {
                'total_anomalies': self.results['is_anomaly'].sum(),
                'anomaly_rate': self.results['is_anomaly'].mean(),
                'high_impact_anomalies': self.results[
                    self.results['anomaly_score'] < -0.5
                ].shape[0]
            }
        })
        
        return patterns
    
    def generate_recommendations(self) -> List[Dict]:
        """Generate intelligent recommendations based on analysis"""
        recommendations = []
        
        # Analyze patterns for recommendations
        patterns = self.analyze_performance_patterns()
        
        # Recommendation 1: Load distribution
        peak_hour = self.results.groupby('hour')['elapsed'].mean().idxmax()
        if patterns['anomaly_summary']['anomaly_rate'] > 0.1:
            recommendations.append({
                'type': 'load_distribution',
                'priority': 'high',
                'message': f"High anomaly rate detected ({patterns['anomaly_summary']['anomaly_rate']:.1%}). Consider load balancing or scaling during peak hours.",
                'action': 'Review infrastructure capacity and consider auto-scaling policies'
            })
        
        # Recommendation 2: Response time optimization
        p95_response = self.results['elapsed'].quantile(0.95)
        if p95_response > 2000:  # 2 seconds
            recommendations.append({
                'type': 'response_time',
                'priority': 'high',
                'message': f"95th percentile response time is {p95_response:.0f}ms, exceeding 2000ms threshold",
                'action': 'Investigate slow endpoints and optimize database queries'
            })
        
        # Recommendation 3: Error rate reduction
        error_rate = 1 - self.results['success'].mean()
        if error_rate > 0.01:  # 1%
            recommendations.append({
                'type': 'error_rate',
                'priority': 'medium',
                'message': f"Error rate is {error_rate:.2%}, exceeding 1% threshold",
                'action': 'Review error logs and fix failing requests'
            })
        
        # Recommendation 4: Test optimization
        test_duration = (self.results['timestamp'].max() - 
                        self.results['timestamp'].min()).total_seconds()
        if test_duration > 3600:  # 1 hour
            recommendations.append({
                'type': 'test_optimization',
                'priority': 'low',
                'message': f"Test duration is {test_duration/3600:.1f} hours. Consider shorter, more frequent tests.",
                'action': 'Implement canary testing and progressive load increases'
            })
        
        return recommendations
    
    def generate_report(self, output_dir: str = './reports') -> Dict:
        """Generate comprehensive performance analysis report"""
        # Ensure output directory exists
        output_path = Path(output_dir)
        output_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        
        # Perform all analyses
        self.load_jmeter_results()
        self.detect_anomalies()
        forecast = self.predict_performance()
        patterns = self.analyze_performance_patterns()
        recommendations = self.generate_recommendations()
        
        # Compile report
        report = {
            'metadata': {
                'analysis_date': datetime.now().isoformat(),
                'results_file': str(self.results_path),
                'total_samples': len(self.results),
                'analysis_duration': (datetime.now() - self.results['timestamp'].min()).total_seconds()
            },
            'summary': {
                'avg_response_time': self.results['elapsed'].mean(),
                'success_rate': self.results['success'].mean(),
                'throughput': len(self.results) / self.results['elapsed'].sum() * 1000,
                'anomaly_count': self.results['is_anomaly'].sum()
            },
            'patterns': patterns,
            'forecast': {
                'next_24h_avg_response': forecast['forecast']['yhat'].iloc[-24:].mean(),
                'peak_prediction': forecast['forecast'].iloc[-24:]['yhat'].max()
            },
            'recommendations': recommendations,
            'visualizations': {
                'anomaly_chart': f"{output_dir}/anomalies.png",
                'forecast_chart': f"{output_dir}/forecast.png",
                'performance_trends': f"{output_dir}/trends.png"
            }
        }
        
        # Save report
        report_file = output_path / 'performance_analysis.json'
        with open(report_file, 'w') as f:
            json.dump(report, f, indent=2, default=str)
        
        # Generate visualizations
        self.generate_visualizations(output_path, forecast)
        
        return report
    
    def generate_visualizations(self, output_path: Path, forecast: Dict):
        """Generate visualization charts"""
        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
        import seaborn as sns
        
        sns.set_style('whitegrid')
        
        # 1. Anomaly detection chart
        plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
        plt.scatter(self.results.index, self.results['elapsed'],
                   c=self.results['anomaly_score'], cmap='RdBu',
                   alpha=0.6, edgecolors='w', linewidth=0.5)
        plt.colorbar(label='Anomaly Score')
        plt.title('Performance Anomalies Detection')
        plt.xlabel('Sample Index')
        plt.ylabel('Response Time (ms)')
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.savefig(output_path / 'anomalies.png', dpi=150)
        plt.close()
        
        # 2. Forecast chart
        fig = self.models['prophet'].plot(forecast['forecast'])
        plt.title('Performance Forecast - Next 24 Hours')
        plt.savefig(output_path / 'forecast.png', dpi=150)
        plt.close()
        
        # 3. Performance trends
        plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
        self.results.set_index('timestamp')['elapsed'].resample('5T').mean().plot()
        plt.title('Response Time Trends')
        plt.xlabel('Time')
        plt.ylabel('Average Response Time (ms)')
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.savefig(output_path / 'trends.png', dpi=150)
        plt.close()

# Main execution
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage
    analyzer = PerformanceAnalyzer("results.jtl")
    report = analyzer.generate_report("./analysis-report")
    
    print("Performance Analysis Complete!")
    print(f"Total samples analyzed: {report['metadata']['total_samples']}")
    print(f"Average response time: {report['summary']['avg_response_time']:.0f}ms")
    print(f"Success rate: {report['summary']['success_rate']:.2%}")
    print(f"Anomalies detected: {report['summary']['anomaly_count']}")
    
    print("\nTop Recommendations:")
    for i, rec in enumerate(report['recommendations'][:3], 1):
        print(f"{i}. [{rec['priority'].upper()}] {rec['message']}")

content.title: What is Gatling and Why Use It?
content.explanation:
Gatling is a modern load testing tool that uses code (Scala DSL) to define performance tests. Unlike GUI tools, Gatling tests are version-controlled, maintainable, and developer-friendly. **Why Gatling?** ✅ **Code-first approach** - Tests are source code ✅ **High performance** - Low resource consumption ✅ **Great reports** - Beautiful HTML reports out of the box ✅ **Developer friendly** - Integrates with build tools **Gatling Architecture**: ```mermaid graph LR A[Scala DSL Script] --> B[Gatling Recorder]
optional B --> C[Simulation Class] C --> D[Gatling Engine] D --> E[HTML Reports] D --> F[Metrics Storage] ``` **Three Main Components**: 1. **Recorder** - Record browser actions (optional) 2. **Engine** - Executes the simulation 3. **Reports** - Generates detailed HTML reports

interactive.question: What is the main advantage of Gatling's code-first approach?
options: Tests can be version-controlled and maintained like code
It has a better user interface
interactive.explanation: Gatling tests are written in Scala DSL, which means they can be version-controlled, reviewed, refactored, and maintained just like any other source code in your project.

content.title: Understanding Gatling DSL
content.explanation:
Gatling uses a Scala-based Domain Specific Language (DSL) that's designed to be readable even if you don't know Scala. Think of it as structured English.

**Basic Building Blocks**:
```scala
// 1. Import packages (always start with these)
import io.gatling.core.Predef._
import io.gatling.http.Predef._

// 2. HTTP Protocol configuration
val httpProtocol = http
  .baseUrl("https://api.example.com")

// 3. Define a Scenario (user journey)
val myScenario = scenario("My First Scenario")
  .exec(http("Get Homepage")  // Name this request
    .get("/"))                // HTTP GET request
  .pause(1)                   // Wait 1 second

// 4. Setup the Simulation
setUp(
  myScenario.inject(atOnceUsers(1)) // 1 user starts immediately
).protocols(httpProtocol)           // Use our HTTP config
```

**Key Concepts**:
• **Simulation** - Main test class (extends `Simulation`)
• **Scenario** - User journey/flow
• **HTTP Protocol** - Configuration (URLs, headers, etc.)
• **exec()** - Execute an action (HTTP request, pause, etc.)
• **inject()** - How many users and when
content.analogy:
Think of Gatling DSL like cooking:
- **Simulation** = The complete recipe
- **Scenario** = Step-by-step instructions
- **exec()** = Individual cooking steps
- **Protocol** = Kitchen setup and tools

content.title: Essential Gatling Components
content.explanation:
Now that you've run your first test, let's explore Gatling's powerful features. These are the tools you'll use for real-world testing. **Three Core Pillars of Gatling**: ```mermaid graph TD A[Gatling Test] --> B[1. Data Management] A --> C[2. User Behavior] A --> D[3. Load Patterns] B --> B1[Feeders
CSV, JSON, JDBC] B --> B2[Session Variables
Save/Extract data] C --> C1[Scenarios
User journeys] C --> C2[Checks
Validations] C --> C3[Pauses
Think times] D --> D1[Injection Profiles
How users arrive] D --> D2[Assertions
Pass/Fail criteria] ``` **Key Features to Master**: 1. **Feeders** - Provide test data to virtual users 2. **Checks** - Validate responses 3. **Injection Profiles** - Control user load patterns 4. **Assertions** - Define test pass/fail criteria
content.tip: 💡 Pro Tip: Gatling's real power comes from combining these features. Start simple, add one feature at a time, and test as you go.

content.caption: 🛒 Complete E-commerce Simulation
content.code:
import io.gatling.core.Predef._
import io.gatling.http.Predef._
import scala.concurrent.duration._

class EcommerceSimulation extends Simulation {

  // === 1. HTTP CONFIGURATION ===
  val httpProtocol = http
    .baseUrl("https://api.store.example.com")
    .acceptHeader("application/json")
    .acceptEncodingHeader("gzip, deflate")
    .userAgentHeader("Mozilla/5.0 Gatling")
    .shareConnections  // Reuse connections for performance
  
  // === 2. FEEDERS ===
  val userFeeder = csv("data/users.csv").circular
  val productFeeder = csv("data/products.csv").random
  val searchTerms = Array("laptop", "phone", "tablet", "watch").circular
  
  // === 3. SCENARIOS ===
  
  // Scenario 1: Casual Browser (70% of users)
  val browserScenario = scenario("Casual Browser")
    .feed(searchTerms)
    .exec(http("Homepage")
      .get("/")
      .check(status.is(200)))
    .pause(2.seconds, 5.seconds)  // Random pause 2-5s
    
    .exec(http("Search Products")
      .get("/products/search?q=${searchTerm}")
      .check(status.is(200))
      .check(jsonPath("$.products[0].id").saveAs("productId")))
    .pause(1.second)
    
    .exec(http("View Product Details")
      .get("/products/${productId}")
      .check(status.is(200))
      .check(jsonPath("$.inStock").is("true")))
    .pause(3.seconds, 7.seconds)
  
  // Scenario 2: Serious Buyer (25% of users)
  val buyerScenario = scenario("Serious Buyer")
    .feed(userFeeder)
    .feed(productFeeder)
    
    .exec(http("Login")
      .post("/auth/login")
      .body(StringBody("""
        {"email": "${email}", "password": "${password}"}
      """))
      .check(status.is(200))
      .check(jsonPath("$.token").saveAs("authToken")))
    .pause(1.second)
    
    .exec(http("Add to Cart")
      .post("/cart/items")
      .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${authToken}")
      .body(StringBody("""
        {"productId": "${productId}", "quantity": 1}
      """))
      .check(status.is(201))
      .check(jsonPath("$.cartId").saveAs("cartId")))
    .pause(2.seconds)
    
    .exec(http("View Cart")
      .get("/cart/${cartId}")
      .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${authToken}")
      .check(status.is(200)))
    .pause(2.seconds, 4.seconds)
    
    .exec(http("Checkout")
      .post("/orders")
      .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${authToken}")
      .body(StringBody("""
        {
          "cartId": "${cartId}",
          "payment": {"type": "credit", "last4": "4242"}
        }
      """))
      .check(status.is(201))
      .check(jsonPath("$.orderId").saveAs("orderId")))
    .pause(5.seconds)  // Payment processing time
    
    .exec(http("Order Confirmation")
      .get("/orders/${orderId}")
      .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${authToken}")
      .check(status.is(200))
      .check(jsonPath("$.status").is("confirmed")))
  
  // Scenario 3: Admin (5% of users)
  val adminScenario = scenario("Administrator")
    .feed(userFeeder)
    
    .exec(http("Admin Login")
      .post("/auth/admin/login")
      .body(StringBody("""
        {"email": "${email}", "password": "${password}"}
      """))
      .check(status.is(200))
      .check(jsonPath("$.adminToken").saveAs("adminToken")))
    .pause(1.second)
    
    .exec(http("View Dashboard")
      .get("/admin/dashboard")
      .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${adminToken}")
      .check(status.is(200)))
    .pause(3.seconds)
    
    .exec(http("Get Orders Report")
      .get("/admin/reports/orders/today")
      .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${adminToken}")
      .check(status.is(200)))
  
  // === 4. LOAD INJECTION ===
  setUp(
    // Black Friday peak traffic simulation
    browserScenario.inject(
      nothingFor(10.seconds),                    // Initial
      rampUsersPerSec(1).to(50).during(5.minutes),  // Morning ramp
      constantUsersPerSec(50).during(30.minutes),   // Mid-day
      rampUsersPerSec(50).to(200).during(10.minutes), // Evening spike
      constantUsersPerSec(200).during(15.minutes),  // Peak hour
      rampUsersPerSec(200).to(20).during(5.minutes)  // Wind down
    ),
    
    buyerScenario.inject(
      rampUsers(500).during(10.minutes),
      constantUsersPerSec(5).during(60.minutes)
    ),
    
    adminScenario.inject(
      constantUsersPerSec(0.1).during(60.minutes)  // Few admins
    )
  ).protocols(httpProtocol)
  
  // === 5. ASSERTIONS ===
  .assertions(
    // Global performance requirements
    global.responseTime.max.lt(5000),           // Max < 5s
    global.responseTime.percentile3.lt(2000),   // p95 < 2s
    global.responseTime.percentile4.lt(3000),   // p99 < 3s
    global.successfulRequests.percent.gt(99.5), // > 99.5% success
    
    // Per-request requirements
    details("Checkout").responseTime.mean.lt(3000),     // Checkout mean < 3s
    details("Login").responseTime.percentile3.lt(1000), // Login p95 < 1s
    details("Add to Cart").failedRequests.percent.lt(1), // < 1% errors
    
    // Throughput requirements
    details("Search Products").requestsPerSec.gt(10),   // > 10 req/sec
    
    // Response size (optional)
    details("View Product Details").responseTime.stdDev.lt(500)  // Consistent
  )
  
  // === 6. THROTTLING (Optional) ===
  .throttle(
    reachRps(100).in(10.seconds),    // Gradually reach 100 RPS
    holdFor(1.minute),              // Maintain for 1 minute
    jumpToRps(50),                  // Drop to 50 RPS
    holdFor(30.seconds)             // Maintain
  )
}

content.title: Automating Gatling in CI/CD
content.explanation:
Gatling tests should run automatically in your CI/CD pipeline. This ensures performance is checked with every change. **CI/CD Integration Benefits**: ```mermaid graph LR A[Developer
Commits Code] --> B[CI Pipeline Starts] B --> C[Unit Tests] C --> D[Gatling Performance Tests] D --> E{Performance OK?} E -->|Yes| F[Deploy to Staging] E -->|No| G[Fail Build
Notify Team] F --> H[More Tests] H --> I[Production Deploy] ``` **Integration Options**: 1. **Maven/Gradle** - Build tool integration 2. **Docker** - Containerized execution 3. **Jenkins/GitLab CI** - Pipeline integration 4. **Gatling Enterprise** - Advanced features
content.tip: 💡 Best Practice: Run quick smoke tests on every commit, full load tests nightly, and stress tests before major releases.

content.caption: 📦 Maven Integration
content.code:
<!-- pom.xml for Gatling Maven project -->
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>performance-tests</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0</version>
  
  <properties>
    <gatling.version>3.9.5</gatling.version>
    <scala.version>2.13.10</scala.version>
  </properties>
  
  <dependencies>
    <!-- Gatling dependencies -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.gatling</groupId>
      <artifactId>gatling-app</artifactId>
      <version>${gatling.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.gatling.highcharts</groupId>
      <artifactId>gatling-charts-highcharts</artifactId>
      <version>${gatling.version}</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
  
  <build>
    <sourceDirectory>src/main/scala</sourceDirectory>
    <testSourceDirectory>src/test/scala</testSourceDirectory>
    
    <plugins>
      <!-- Scala compiler -->
      <plugin>
        <groupId>net.alchim31.maven</groupId>
        <artifactId>scala-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>4.8.1</version>
        <executions>
          <execution>
            <goals>
              <goal>compile</goal>
              <goal>testCompile</goal>
            </goals>
          </execution>
        </executions>
      </plugin>
      
      <!-- Gatling Maven Plugin -->
      <plugin>
        <groupId>io.gatling</groupId>
        <artifactId>gatling-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>4.5.0</version>
        <configuration>
          <simulationClass>simulations.EcommerceSimulation</simulationClass>
          <runMultipleSimulations>false</runMultipleSimulations>
          <includes>
            <!-- Run all simulations -->
            <include>**/*Simulation.scala</include>
          </includes>
        </configuration>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>

content.caption: 🔧 GitLab CI Pipeline
content.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - test
  - performance
  - deploy

variables:
  GATLING_HOME: "${CI_PROJECT_DIR}/gatling"
  
# Cache dependencies
cache:
  paths:
    - .m2/repository
    - target/gatling

# Unit tests stage
unit-tests:
  stage: test
  image: maven:3.8-openjdk-11
  script:
    - mvn clean test
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: target/surefire-reports/*.xml

# Performance tests stage
gatling-performance:
  stage: performance
  image: maven:3.8-openjdk-11
  script:
    # Run Gatling tests
    - mvn gatling:test -Dgatling.simulationClass=simulations.EcommerceSimulation
    
    # Generate summary report
    - |
      echo "=== PERFORMANCE TEST SUMMARY ==="
      echo "Last report: $(ls -td target/gatling/*/ | head -1)"
      
      # Extract key metrics (simplified)
      REPORT_DIR=$(ls -td target/gatling/*/ | head -1)
      cat $REPORT_DIR/js/stats.json | grep -E '(meanResponseTime|percentile95|numberOfRequests|meanNumberOfRequestsPerSecond)'
      
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - target/gatling/**/*

# Dockerfile for Gatling
FROM openjdk:11-jre-slim

# Install dependencies

    wget \
    unzip \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Download Gatling
ARG GATLING_VERSION=3.9.5
RUN wget -q -O gatling.zip https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/io/gatling/gatling-bundle/${GATLING_VERSION}/gatling-bundle-${GATLING_VERSION}-bundle.zip \
    && unzip gatling.zip \
    && rm gatling.zip \
    && mv gatling-bundle-${GATLING_VERSION} /gatling

# Copy test files
COPY simulations/ /gatling/user-files/simulations/
COPY data/ /gatling/user-files/data/
COPY resources/ /gatling/user-files/resources/

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /gatling

# Entry point
ENTRYPOINT ["./bin/gatling.sh"]
CMD ["-s", "simulations.EcommerceSimulation"]

examples.title: GitHub Actions Workflow with Performance Gates
examples.code:
name: Performance Testing Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
  schedule:
    # Daily performance regression testing
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'

jobs:
  unit-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      
      - name: Run unit tests
        run: npm test
  
  api-performance:
    needs: unit-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Install k6
        uses: grafana/setup-k6-action@v1
        with:
          version: latest
      
      - name: Run API smoke tests
        run: k6 run --out json=smoke-results.json tests/smoke.js
        env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_API_URL }}
          K6_CLOUD_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.K6_CLOUD_TOKEN }}
      
      - name: Check performance thresholds
        run: |
          # Parse results and check thresholds
          python scripts/check-thresholds.py smoke-results.json
          
          # Upload results as artifact
          echo "Performance test completed"
      
      - name: Upload test results
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        if: always()
        with:
          name: performance-results
          path: smoke-results.json
  
  load-testing:
    needs: api-performance
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Install k6
        uses: grafana/setup-k6-action@v1
      
      - name: Execute load test
        run: k6 cloud tests/load.js
        env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_API_URL }}
          K6_CLOUD_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.K6_CLOUD_TOKEN }}
          K6_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID: ${{ secrets.K6_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID }}
      
      - name: Generate performance report
        run: |
          # Generate markdown report for PR
          python scripts/generate-report.py
          
      - name: Comment on PR with results
        uses: actions/github-script@v6
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require('fs');
            const report = fs.readFileSync('performance-report.md', 'utf8');
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: report
            });
  
  performance-gate:
    needs: load-testing
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check if performance regression
        run: |
          # Compare with baseline
          python scripts/compare-with-baseline.py
          
          # Fail if significant regression
          if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
            echo "Performance regression detected!"
            echo "Please review the performance test results."
            exit 1
          fi

examples.code:
# newrelic.yml - Comprehensive APM configuration
common: &default_settings
  # License and application configuration
  license_key: ${NEW_RELIC_LICENSE_KEY}
  app_name: ${NEW_RELIC_APP_NAME:-My Application}
  
  # Distributed tracing configuration
  distributed_tracing:
    enabled: true
  span_events:
    enabled: true
    harvest_limits:
      harvest_limit: 2000
  
  # Transaction tracing
  transaction_tracer:
    enabled: true
    transaction_threshold: apdex_f
    record_sql: obfuscated
    explain_threshold: 500
    
    # Stack trace configuration
    stack_trace_threshold: 500
    
  # Error collection
  error_collector:
    enabled: true
    ignore_status_codes: 404
    
  # Browser monitoring (RUM)
  browser_monitoring:
    enable: true
    debug: false
    
  # Thread profiling
  thread_profiler:
    enabled: true
    
  # Labels for environment and team
  labels:
    environment: ${ENVIRONMENT:-development}
    team: platform-engineering
    service_tier: critical
    
  # Logging integration
  application_logging:
    enabled: true
    forwarding:
      enabled: true
      max_samples_stored: 10000
    metrics:
      enabled: true
    local_decorating:
      enabled: false
  
  # Custom attributes
  attributes:
    enabled: true
    exclude:
      - request.headers.cookie
      - request.headers.authorization
      - response.headers.set-cookie
    
  # Security settings
  security:
    enabled: true
    
  # High security mode (for compliance)
  high_security: false

# Environment-specific overrides
development:
  <<: *default_settings
  app_name: ${NEW_RELIC_APP_NAME} (Development)
  audit_mode: false
  log_level: info
  
staging:
  <<: *default_settings
  app_name: ${NEW_RELIC_APP_NAME} (Staging)
  audit_mode: false
  log_level: info
  
production:
  <<: *default_settings
  app_name: ${NEW_RELIC_APP_NAME}
  audit_mode: false
  log_level: info
  
  # Production-specific optimizations
  transaction_tracer:
    enabled: true
    transaction_threshold: 1.0
    
  # Span events configuration for production
  span_events:
    enabled: true
    harvest_limits:
      harvest_limit: 10000
      
  # Error collector for production
  error_collector:
    ignore_status_codes: 404, 429
    
  # Custom insights events
  custom_insights_events:
    enabled: true
    max_samples_stored: 10000

# Kubernetes/container specific settings
container:
  <<: *default_settings
  utilization:
    detect_aws: true
    detect_azure: true
    detect_gcp: true
    detect_pcf: true
    detect_docker: true
    detect_kubernetes: true
  
  process_host:
    display_name: ${HOSTNAME}

# JVM arguments for optimal performance
# Java agent startup arguments:
# -javaagent:/path/to/newrelic.jar
# -Dnewrelic.config.file=/path/to/newrelic.yml
# -Dnewrelic.environment=production

# Custom instrumentation example
custom_instrumentation:
  - name: CustomKafkaConsumer
    metric_name: MessageBroker/Kafka/Consume/
    transaction_type: background
    pointcut:
      - type: method
        class_name: com.company.messaging.KafkaConsumer
        method_name: consume
        method_params:
          - "org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecord"
    attributes:
      capture:
        - class_name: com.company.messaging.KafkaConsumer
          attributes:
            - property_name: topic
              attribute_name: message.topic
            - property_name: partition
              attribute_name: message.partition
            - argument_index: 0
              attribute_name: message.key
              getter:
                class_name: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecord
                method_name: key
                method_params: []

examples.title: Prometheus SLO Rules & Recording Rules
examples.code:
# prometheus-rules.yml - SLO configuration for Prometheus

groups:
  - name: slo-rules
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      
      # Availability SLO for API endpoints (99.9% target)
      - record: slo:api_availability:ratio
        expr: >
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api", status!~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m]))
        labels:
          slo: "api-availability"
          target: "0.999"
          severity: "critical"
          
      # Latency SLO for p95 < 500ms
      - record: slo:api_latency:ratio
        expr: >
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api", le="0.5"}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="api"}[5m]))
        labels:
          slo: "api-latency"
          target: "0.95"  # 95% of requests under 500ms
          severity: "critical"
          
      # Error budget remaining
      - record: slo:api_availability:error_budget_remaining
        expr: (1 - (1 - slo:api_availability:ratio) / (1 - 0.999)) * 100
        labels:
          slo: "api-availability"
          
      # Burn rate calculation (for alerting)
      - record: slo:api_availability:burn_rate_5m
        expr: >
          (1 - slo:api_availability:ratio)
          /
          (1 - 0.999)  # Error budget consumption rate
        labels:
          slo: "api-availability"
          window: "5m"
          
      - record: slo:api_availability:burn_rate_1h
        expr: >
          (1 - 
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api", status!~"5.."}[1h]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[1h]))
          )
          /
          (1 - 0.999)
        labels:
          slo: "api-availability"
          window: "1h"
          
      # Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alert rules
  - name: slo-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: APIAvailabilityErrorBudgetBurn
        expr: >
          slo:api_availability:burn_rate_5m > 14.4
          or
          slo:api_availability:burn_rate_1h > 3
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          team: platform
          slo: api-availability
        annotations:
          summary: "API availability error budget burning fast"
          description: >
            API availability SLO (99.9%) error budget is being consumed too quickly.
            Burn rate: {{ $labels.window }} = {{ $value | humanize }}x faster than allowed.
            Current availability: {{ printf "%.2f" (query("slo:api_availability:ratio")) }}%
          runbook: "https://runbook.company.com/api-availability"
          dashboard: "https://grafana.company.com/d/api-slo"
          
      - alert: APILatencySLOViolation
        expr: slo:api_latency:ratio < 0.95
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          team: platform
          slo: api-latency
        annotations:
          summary: "API latency SLO violation"
          description: >
            API latency SLO (p95 < 500ms) is being violated.
            Current ratio: {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}
            Target: 95%
          dashboard: "https://grafana.company.com/d/api-slo"
          
      # Business transaction SLOs
      - record: slo:checkout_success:ratio
        expr: >
          sum(rate(business_transactions_total{job="api", transaction="checkout", status="success"}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(business_transactions_total{job="api", transaction="checkout"}[5m]))
        labels:
          slo: "checkout-success"
          target: "0.995"  # 99.5% success rate
          
      # Custom business metric tracking
      - record: revenue:processed:rate
        expr: sum(rate(business_transactions_total{job="api", transaction="purchase", status="success"}[5m]))
          * on() group_left()
          avg(business_transaction_value{job="api"})
        labels:
          metric: "revenue-processed"
          unit: "USD/hour"
          
  # Synthetic monitoring rules
  - name: synthetic-monitoring
    rules:
      - record: synthetic:api_health:success_rate
        expr: >
          sum(rate(synthetic_check_total{check="api-health", result="success"}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(synthetic_check_total{check="api-health"}[5m]))
        labels:
          check: "api-health"
          frequency: "1m"
          
      # Uptime calculation
      - record: uptime:api:percentage
        expr: synthetic:api_health:success_rate * 100
        labels:
          service: "api"
          target: "99.95"

content.title: Mobile Performance Engineering
content.content: Mobile performance engineering is a specialized discipline focused on optimizing mobile applications for variable network conditions, limited device resources, diverse hardware capabilities, and user experience expectations specific to mobile platforms.
keyPoints: Mobile performance extends beyond traditional metrics to include battery life and thermal impact
Network variability is a primary performance determinant in mobile environments
Device fragmentation requires testing across multiple hardware configurations
Mobile user expectations prioritize responsiveness and offline capabilities
App store optimization includes performance as a key ranking factor
content.details: Mobile applications operate in fundamentally different environments than web or desktop applications, facing constraints like intermittent connectivity, limited battery life, diverse screen sizes, and varying hardware capabilities. Performance engineering for mobile requires specialized approaches that account for these unique challenges while maintaining optimal user experiences.

content.title: Performance Test Automation Framework
content.content: A performance test automation framework is a structured, reusable foundation that provides standardized components, patterns, and practices for designing, executing, and analyzing performance tests at scale. It transforms ad-hoc testing into an engineering discipline.
keyPoints: Frameworks provide consistency and standardization across test suites
Modular architecture enables component reuse and maintainability
Abstracted layers separate test logic from execution details
Configuration management enables environment-agnostic testing
Extensible design supports evolving testing requirements
content.details: Enterprise performance test frameworks are engineered to handle complex testing scenarios across multiple environments, applications, and teams. They incorporate software engineering best practices, design patterns, and architectural principles to create maintainable, scalable, and reliable testing infrastructure that evolves with the applications they test.

content.title: Test Data Management Implementation Process
steps: Step 1: Data Requirements Analysis - Identify test data needs, analyze data models and relationships, define data characteristics and distributions, establish data privacy requirements
Step 2: Data Strategy Design - Select data management approach, design data generation algorithms, plan data storage and retrieval, define data lifecycle management
Step 3: Implementation - Develop data generation utilities, implement data masking/anonymization, create data provisioning APIs, build data quality validation
Step 4: Integration - Integrate with test framework, implement data cleanup mechanisms, establish data versioning, create monitoring and reporting
Step 5: Optimization - Analyze data usage patterns, optimize generation performance, implement caching strategies, refine data characteristics based on test results

items.definition: Implement layered configuration with defaults, environment-specific overrides, and test-specific customizations to manage complexity and promote reuse.
Validate configuration at load time with schema validation, value range checks, and dependency validation to catch errors before test execution.
Secure handling of sensitive configuration (credentials, API keys) using encrypted storage, environment variables, or dedicated secret management services.
Version control configuration alongside test code with change tracking, rollback capabilities, and audit trails for configuration changes.
Support for runtime configuration updates without restarting tests, enabling adaptive testing and parameter adjustments during execution.
Reusable configuration templates for common test scenarios with parameterization and inheritance to reduce duplication and ensure consistency.
Comprehensive documentation of configuration options, their purposes, valid values, and examples to support framework users and maintainers.
Automated testing of configuration combinations to validate correctness and identify conflicts or invalid combinations before production use.

content.title: CI/CD Integration Implementation Process
steps: Step 1: Pipeline Analysis - Analyze existing CI/CD pipelines, identify integration points, define performance testing stages, establish quality gates
Step 2: Integration Design - Design automated test execution triggers, define result analysis and decision logic, plan feedback mechanisms, establish failure handling
Step 3: Implementation - Implement pipeline integrations, create automated test execution jobs, develop result processing and analysis, implement notification systems
Step 4: Testing & Validation - Test integration workflows, validate decision logic, verify notification systems, conduct end-to-end testing
Step 5: Rollout & Monitoring - Roll out to pilot projects, monitor integration performance, gather user feedback, refine based on usage patterns

items.definition: Implement different test types at different pipeline stages (smoke tests on PRs, integration tests on merge, full load tests on staging, canary tests on production).
Dynamic quality gates based on code changes, risk assessment, and historical performance data rather than fixed thresholds for all scenarios.
Minimize test execution time for early pipeline stages through optimized test design, parallel execution, and intelligent test selection.
Automated analysis of test failures with root cause suggestions, historical comparisons, and remediation recommendations to accelerate resolution.
Efficient use of testing resources through containerization, spot instances, resource pooling, and automated scaling based on test requirements.
Automated rollback procedures triggered by performance test failures with proper notification, impact assessment, and remediation tracking.
Tracking and visualization of performance debt with prioritization, ownership assignment, and progress tracking integrated into development workflows.
Tools and processes that facilitate collaboration between development, testing, and operations teams around performance testing results and improvements.
